label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
For every $k\geqslant 2$, the smooth manifolds
\[
 M_k:=\#_k({\mathbb S^2}\times {\mathbb S^2}),\qquad \text{ and }\qquad
 N_k:=k\mathbb{CP}^{2}\#(2k+1)\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^{2}
\]
admit Einstein metrics with positive scalar curvature.
head: environment

label: thm:angle
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:angle}
For either initial metric $g_1$, there is a family
$(g_\beta)_{0<\beta\leqslant1}$ starting at $g_1$, with
\[
 \operatorname{Ric}(g_\beta)=3g_\beta\quad\text{on }M\setminus\Sigma,\quad \text{ and }\quad\text{ conical singularity of angle $2\pi\beta$ along $\Sigma$}.
\]
They are smooth on $M\setminus\Sigma$ and invariant under the torus action and under the finite  group $\mathcal G$ of Section~\ref{subsec:symmetries}. They depend smoothly on $\beta$ in the weighted spaces of Section~\ref{sec:spaces}, in the sense of Corollary~\ref{cor:local}.

label: prop:Ricci
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Ricci curvature is computed in \cite[Section~2.1, (2.6), (2.10), and~(2.17)]{LS25}:
with $J:=G^{-1}dG$ it gives
\[
 \operatorname{Ric}_g|_{T\Omega}=\operatorname{Ric}_h-\operatorname{Hess}_h\log\rho
                    -\tfrac14\operatorname{tr}(J\otimes J),
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad G^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g^{\rm v}=-\tfrac1{2\rho}\operatorname{div}_h(\rho J).
\]
Our normalization satisfies
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 J&=d\ell\,I+\Phi^{-1}d\Phi,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(\Phi^{-1}d\Phi)=0,\\
 \tfrac14\operatorname{tr}(J\otimes J)
 &=\tfrac12d\ell^2+\tfrac12\Phi^*g_{\mathbb H^2},\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \sqrt{\det g}=\rho\sqrt{\det h}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
These identities give \eqref{eq:matrix-ricci}. Then $S_g=\operatorname{tr}_h(\operatorname{Ric}_g|_{T\Omega})+\operatorname{tr}(G^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g^{\rm v})$ and $dV_g=\rho\,dA_h\,d\phi_1\,d\phi_2$ give \eqref{eq:scalar-volume} and
\eqref{eq:geometric-laplacian}.

label: prop:reduced
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using the decomposition in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:Ricci}, the vertical equation and \eqref{eq:matrix-ricci} give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 6=\operatorname{tr}(G^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g^{\rm v})
 &=-\rho^{-1}\operatorname{div}_h(\rho\nabla_h\ell)
 =-\rho^{-1}\Delta_h\rho,\\
 0=(G^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g^{\rm v})^\circ
 &=-\frac{1}{2\rho}\operatorname{div}_h(\rho \Phi^{-1}d\Phi).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The equation $(G^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g^{\rm v})^\circ=0$ becomes the equation for $\Phi$ in \eqref{eq:matrix-reduced} after multiplication by $e^{2a}$, since  $\rho^{-1}\operatorname{div}_h(\rho\Phi^{-1}d\Phi)=\Phi^{-1}\bigl(\tau_h(\Phi)+d\Phi(\nabla_h\ell)\bigr)$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-calculus}(iii).
For the scalar equation $S_g=12$, use the scalar-curvature identity \eqref{eq:scalar-volume}:
\[
 12=2K_h+12+\tfrac12(|d\ell|_h^2-|d\Phi|_h^2),
 \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad 4K_h=|d\Phi|_h^2-|d\ell|_h^2.
\]
The equation for $a$ in \eqref{eq:matrix-reduced} is obtained using the 2D curvature formula
\[
 e^{2a}K_h=K_\gamma-\Delta_\gamma a
 \qquad \text{ with }h=e^{2a}\gamma.
\]

title: Remark

title: Remark
body_md:
Li and Sun only impose bounded hyperbolic distance from the rod and corner models, and \textit{recover} smoothness from the Ricci-flat equations after adjusting periods and coordinates \cite[Section~4.2]{LS25}.
Here regularity is \textit{prescribed} in fixed charts also for variations that do not satisfy the Einstein equation. These prescribed conditions dictate some of our choices of function spaces.

label: lem:central-modes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:central-modes}
Let $F$ be a $\mathcal G$-invariant function on $B_o\setminus\{o\}$, such as $f$, $b$, $\rho$ or $a$, or one of the equivariant maps $\xi^o$ and $U=\Pi_{\Phi_o}\Phi$. Then $F_j\neq0$ only for $j\in2\mathbb Z$, and $\xi^o_0=U_0=0$. In particular, every harmonic mode $R^{|j|/\beta}e^{ij\theta}$ of $F$ with $j\neq0$ has degree at least $2/\beta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The rotation $\mathsf r$ acts by $\theta\mapsto\theta+2\pi/m$ and on the values of $F$ by a linear map $C$ commuting with $\Pi_{\Phi_o}$, so that $F(R,\theta+2\pi/m)=C\,F(R,\theta)$. Taking Fourier coefficients, we obtain
\[
 \bigl(e^{2\pi ij/m}I-C\bigr)F_j=0,
\]
so $F_j\neq0$ only if $e^{2\pi ij/m}$ is an eigenvalue of $C$.
\begin{itemize}
\item For invariant functions $C=1$, so $j\in m\mathbb Z$.
\item In the square, $U$ and $\xi^o$ lie on the diagonal line of $T_{\Phi_o}\mathbb H^2$, where $C=-1$ because $\mathsf r=\mathsf r_x\mathsf e$ exchanges the two circles, so $j\in4\mathbb Z+2$.
\item In the hexagon, $C(V)=\mathsf A^{-\mathsf T}V\mathsf A^{-1}$ by \eqref{eq:hexagon-equivariance}. In the coordinates $V=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}v_1&v_2\\v_2&-v_1-v_2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ of $T_{\Phi_o}\mathbb H^2=\{\operatorname{tr}(\Phi_o^{-1}V)=0\}$, it reads $C(v_1,v_2)=(-v_1-v_2,v_1)$ with eigenvalues $e^{\pm2\pi i/3}$, hence $j\in6\mathbb Z\pm2$.
\end{itemize}
Together with \eqref{eq:central-indicial-equation}, this gives the stated degrees.

title: Remark

\label{rem:friedrichs}
As in \cite[Section~5.4]{MW17}, we use the Friedrichs extension of $\Delta_{\gamma_\beta}$: the conditions \eqref{eq:central-domain} exclude $\log R$ and the negative powers in the expansion of harmonic modes, which would make the energy $\int_{\{R<R_0\}}|du|^2_{\gamma_\beta}\,dA_{\gamma_\beta}$ infinite.

label: lem:regularized-chart
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:regularized-chart}
At a corner, put  $\widehat a:=a+c_\gamma$ and $\widehat\Phi:=\widehat\rho^{-1}\widehat G$. The exponential chart \eqref{eq:local-chart} reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:matrix-chart-differential}
 \widehat\ell=\widehat\ell_*+f,\qquad
 \widehat\Phi=\operatorname{Exp}_{\widehat\Phi_*}\bigl(\xi_s\,e_s(\widehat\Phi_*)+\xi_\perp\,e_\perp(\widehat\Phi_*)\bigr),\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \widehat a=\widehat a_*+b.
\end{equation}
The map $q\mapsto(\widehat\ell-\widehat\ell_*,\widehat s-\widehat s_*,\widehat\omega-\widehat\omega_*,\widehat a-\widehat a_*)$ is a smooth diffeomorphism between neighborhoods of $0$ in $C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}\times C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}\times C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}\times C^{2,\alpha}$, with differential $(f,\xi_s,e^{\widehat s_*}\xi_\perp,b)$ at $q=0$. In particular, for $q$ near $0$, $\|q\|_{\mathcal X(U_c)}$ is equivalent to
\[
 \|\widehat\ell-\widehat\ell_*\|_{C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}}+\|\widehat s-\widehat s_*\|_{C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}}+\|\widehat\omega-\widehat\omega_*\|_{C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}}+\|\widehat a-\widehat a_*\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}.
\]
On the axes, $\widehat s-\widehat s_*=\xi_s$ and $\widehat\omega=\widehat\omega_*$, so the boundary conditions of \eqref{eq:corner-domain} are exactly the angle equalities \eqref{eq:angle-equalities}. The same holds with bars at a rod, with \eqref{eq:conic-boundary}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Put $\mathsf D:=(xy)^{1/2}\operatorname{diag}(x^{-1},y^{-1})$, so that $\det\mathsf D=1$ and  $\widehat\Phi=\mathsf D\Phi\mathsf D$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-calculus}(iii), the congruence $S\mapsto\mathsf DS\mathsf D$ is an isometry of $\mathbb H^2$  commuting with \eqref{eq:matrix-exp}. It is the dilation $z\mapsto\frac{x}yz$  of Section~\ref{sec:smoothness}, which preserves the frame \eqref{eq:target-rod-frame}, and this gives \eqref{eq:matrix-chart-differential} and the differential. The reflections  across the axes act on the regularized coordinates by $\widehat\omega\mapsto-\widehat\omega$, which fixes $e_s$ and reverses $e_\perp$. Since $\widehat s_*$ is even, $\widehat\omega_*$ is odd  and $\operatorname{Exp}$ depends smoothly on its base point, the map preserves the parities, and the inverse function theorem gives the diffeomorphism and the equivalence of norms. On an axis, $\xi_\perp=0$ by oddness, and $\tau\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_{\widehat\Phi_*}(\tau e_s)$ is the vertical line $\{\widehat\omega=\widehat\omega_*\}$, parametrized by arclength $\widehat s$. So $\widehat s-\widehat s_*=\xi_s$ and $\widehat\omega=\widehat\omega_*$  there, and subtracting the angle equalities  of $g_*$ from those of $g_{\beta,q}$ gives the last claim. At a rod, use $\mathsf D:=x^{1/2}\operatorname{diag}(x^{-1},1)$.

label: rem:corner-compatibility
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:corner-compatibility}
The corner condition \eqref{eq:corner-compatibility} is necessary for the $C^{2,\alpha}$ Dirichlet problem: if $u\in C^2(\{x,y\geqslant0\})$ vanishes on both axes, then we have
\[
 \partial_x^2u(0)=\partial_y^2u(0)=0,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Delta_0u(0)=0,
\]
and the following lemma, based on \cite[Theorem~6.4.2.5]{Gri85}, shows that it is also sufficient.
head: environment

label: lem:grisvard
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:grisvard}
Let $U$ be a relative neighborhood of the corner $c$ in a quadrant chart $\{x,y\geqslant0\}$, let $\gamma=e^{2c_\gamma}|dw|^2$ with $c_\gamma$ smooth and even, and let $0<\alpha<1$. Let $u\in H^1(U)$ vanish on $\{x=0\}$ and on $\{y=0\}$, and solve $\Delta_\gamma u=F$ weakly, with $F\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$ and $F(c)=0$. Then, for every relative neighborhood $U'$ of $c$ with compact closure in $U$, we have
\[
 \|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(U')}\leqslant C\bigl(\|F\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(U)}+\|u\|_{L^2(U)}\bigr).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The odd reflections of $u$ and $F$ across both axes solve a weak equation near $c$ with bounded right-hand side, so  $u\in C^{1,\alpha}$ near $c$  by \cite[Theorem~8.17 and Corollary~8.36]{GT01}. The local corner expansion of \cite[Theorems~6.4.2.4 and~6.4.2.5]{Gri85}, applied to $\Delta_0u=e^{2c_\gamma}F$, gives $u=v+\lambda\operatorname{Im}(w^2\log w)$ near $c$,  with $w=x+iy$, $v\in C^{2,\alpha}$, and the stated bound for $v$ and $\lambda$. The function  $\operatorname{Im}(w^2\log w)$ is harmonic, vanishes on $\{y=0\}$ and equals $-\frac{\pi}{2}y^2$ on $\{x=0\}$, so the zero boundary values  imply $v_{xx}(c)=0$ and $v_{yy}(c)=\pi\lambda$. Consequently $e^{2c_\gamma(c)}F(c)=\Delta_0v(c)=\pi\lambda$, and  $F(c)=0$ eliminates the logarithmic term. Away from the corner,  the estimate is the boundary Schauder estimate \cite[Lemma~6.18 and Corollary~6.7]{GT01}.

label: lem:reduced-map
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Axes.} Use the corner regularizations of \eqref{eq:regularized-corner-matrix}. By  Lemma~\ref{lem:regularized-chart}, they depend smoothly on $q$, with $\widehat\ell,\widehat s$ even, $\widehat\omega$ odd in each variable and $\widehat a\in C^{2,\alpha}$, and they satisfy the angle equalities \eqref{eq:angle-equalities}. 

By Lemma~\ref{lem:regularized-equations}, the regularized form \eqref{cmp:nonlinear-first-residuals} of the reduced equations \eqref{eq:matrix-reduced} defines smooth maps into the spaces \eqref{eq:conic-spaces}, and its transverse component $e^{2c_\gamma}\mathcal H_\perp$ is odd in each variable.

For the condition \eqref{eq:corner-compatibility}, evaluate the last line of \eqref{cmp:nonlinear-first-residuals} at $c$. At $c$, \eqref{eq:divided-even} gives $x^{-1}\partial_x(\widehat\ell+\widehat s)=\partial_x^2(\widehat\ell+\widehat s)$ and $y^{-1}\partial_y(\widehat\ell-\widehat s)=\partial_y^2(\widehat\ell-\widehat s)$, the first derivatives of the even functions $\widehat\ell$ and $\widehat s$ vanish, and $A_\Phi(c)=0$ by \eqref{eq:connection-regularity}. So \eqref{eq:corner-jets} gives
\[
 e^{2c_\gamma(c)}\mathcal E_3(c)=\Delta_0\widehat a(c)-\tfrac12\partial_x^2(\widehat\ell+\widehat s)(c)-\tfrac12\partial_y^2(\widehat\ell-\widehat s)(c)=0.
\]
At a rod, $\bar\omega$ and $e^{2c_\gamma}\mathcal H_\perp$ are odd in $x$.

\emph{Center.} For functions or $T_{\Phi_o}\mathbb H^2$-valued maps $F,\widetilde F$ with $F-F(o),\widetilde F-\widetilde F(o)\in R^\nu C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, we have $dF,d\widetilde F\in R^{\nu-1}C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, so  \eqref{eq:weighted-product} and the inclusion $R^{2\nu-2}C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}\subset R^{\nu-2}C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, valid as $\nu>0$,  bound $dF\cdot d\widetilde F$ in $R^{\nu-2}C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$ by the product of the norms of $F-F(o)$ and $\widetilde F-\widetilde F(o)$ in $R^\nu C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, and $\Delta_{\gamma_\beta}$ maps constants plus $R^\nu C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$ to $R^{\nu-2}C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$.

\emph{Interior.} Interior charts use ordinary H\"older multiplication. All coefficients depend smoothly on $\beta$ in the fixed coordinates, and \eqref{eq:conic-map} preserves the finite symmetries. This proves the smooth mapping into $\mathcal Y$.

label: prop:recovery
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:recovery}
Let $(\beta,q)\in J\times\mathcal U_0$ satisfy $\mathcal E(\beta,q)=0$, and let $g=g_{\beta,q}$. Then $\operatorname{Ric}_g=3g$ on $\pi^{-1}(\Omega\setminus\{o\})$, and $\partial_na=0$ on each rod, where $n$ is the $\gamma_\beta$-unit normal.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $T:=\rho(\operatorname{Ric}_g-3g)|_{T\Omega}$.  Since \eqref{eq:matrix-reduced} is elliptic with smooth coefficients on $\Omega\setminus\{o\}$, interior Schauder estimates \cite[Theorem~6.2]{GT01} make $q$, hence $g$ and $T$, smooth there, and the identities \eqref{eq:residual-tensor} below hold in the classical sense in $\Omega\setminus\{o\}$.

\emph{Step 1: the equations for $T$.}  By \eqref{eq:matrix-ricci} and Proposition~\ref{prop:reduced} we have $\operatorname{tr}_hT=0$. Since the scalar curvature of $g$ is constant, the contracted Bianchi identity gives $\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{Ric}_g-3g)=0$, and we compute
\[
 \operatorname{div}_hT=\rho\,\bigl(\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{Ric}_g-3g)\bigr)|_{T\Omega}=0.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:matrix-ricci}, this gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residual-tensor}
 T=-\rho\bigl(\operatorname{Hess}_h\ell+\tfrac12d\ell^2+\tfrac12\Phi^*g_{\mathbb H^2}\bigr)^\circ,\qquad \operatorname{tr}_hT=0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{div}_hT=0.
\end{equation}
It remains to prove $T=0$.

\emph{Step 2: behavior at the sides, the corners and $o$.} In dimension two, the equations $\operatorname{tr}_hT=0$ and $\operatorname{div}_hT=0$ are conformally invariant by \cite[Section~3.3, Proposition~2]{MW17}. We shall apply $\operatorname{tr}T=0$ and $\operatorname{div} T=0$ with the Euclidean metric $|d\zeta|^2$ of \eqref{eq:normalized-quotient}, and we write $p_c:=\zeta(c)\in\partial\mathbb D$ for the image of a corner $c$. 

At a rod, in the rod coordinates $(x,y)$ of \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-side}, with the rod regularizations $\rho=xe^{\bar\ell}$, $s=-\log x+\bar s$, $\omega=\frac{\bar\omega}x$ and $h=e^{2\bar a}|dw|^2$, we have $d\ell=\frac{dx}x+d\bar\ell$, $ds=-\frac{dx}x+d\bar s$ and $\operatorname{Hess}_0\log x+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{dx}x)^2+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{dx}x)^2=0$, where the two squares come from $\frac{1}{2}d\ell^2$ and $\frac{1}{2}ds^2$. By \eqref{eq:connection-regularity}, we also have $A_\Phi=O(x)$.
Using $(\operatorname{Hess}_hF)^\circ=(\operatorname{Hess}_0F-2d\bar a\,dF)^\circ$ and $\Phi^*g_{\mathbb H^2}=ds^2+A_\Phi^2$ in \eqref{eq:residual-tensor}, the terms of order $x^{-2}$ cancel by the identity for $\operatorname{Hess}_0\log x$ above, and, since $\rho=xe^{\bar\ell}$, this leaves
\[
 T=-e^{\bar\ell}\bigl(dx\,d(\bar\ell-\bar s-2\bar a)\bigr)^\circ+O(x).
\]
Since $\partial_x\bar\ell=\partial_x\bar s=0$ on $\{x=0\}$, $T$ extends continuously to $\{x=0\}$, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residual-boundary}
 T(\partial_x,\partial_y)|_{x=0}=e^{\bar\ell}\,\partial_y\bigl(\bar a-\tfrac12(\bar\ell-\bar s)\bigr)|_{x=0}=0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 T(\partial_x,\partial_x)|_{x=0}=e^{\bar\ell}\,\partial_x\bar a|_{x=0}.
\end{equation}
The first equality uses the angle equality $2\bar a=\bar\ell-\bar s$ on $\{x=0\}$ of \eqref{eq:angle-equalities}, and, once $T=0$ is known, the second gives the missing Neumann condition.

At a corner, use $w=x+iy$, $r_c:=|w|$ and $h=e^{2\widehat a}|dw|^2$, let $\operatorname{Hess}_0$ denote the Hessian for $|dw|^2$, and put $L_+:=\log(xy)$ and $L_-:=\log(y/x)$. All terms of \eqref{eq:residual-tensor} involving only $L_\pm$ cancel as in the flat case by
\[
 \operatorname{Hess}_0L_++\tfrac12dL_+^2+\tfrac12dL_-^2=0.
\]
 The remaining terms of \eqref{eq:residual-tensor} contain bounded second derivatives, or one logarithmic derivative multiplied by a first derivative which is $O(r_c)$ uniformly up to both axes: evenness gives $d\widehat\ell(c)=d\widehat s(c)=0$, \eqref{eq:corner-jets} gives $d\widehat a(c)=0$, and \eqref{eq:connection-regularity} gives $|A_\Phi|_0=O(r_c)$. Since $\rho=O(r_c^2)$  and $\rho(|dL_+|_0+|dL_-|_0)=O(r_c)$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residual-corner}
 |T|_{|dw|^2}=O(r_c^2),\qquad\text{and}\qquad |T|_{|d\zeta|^2}=O(1).
\end{equation}
For the second bound, $\zeta-p_c=\psi_c(w^2)$ near $c$, with $\psi_c$ holomorphic, $\psi_c(0)=0$ and $\psi_c'(0)\neq0$, since $\zeta$ maps the right angle  at $c$ conformally onto a neighborhood of $p_c$ in $\overline{\mathbb D}$. So $|d\zeta|/|dw|$ is bounded above and below by positive  multiples of $r_c$.

Near $o$, $\zeta$ is a conformal coordinate with $d\zeta(o)\neq0$, so \eqref{eq:fixed-cone-identification} gives $R=|\zeta|^\beta e^{\kappa}$ near $o$, with $\kappa$ smooth. From now on, the subscript $0$ refers to the Euclidean metric $|d\zeta|^2$, not to $|dw|^2$. Write $h=e^{2a_\zeta}|d\zeta|^2$ near $o$, with $|da_\zeta|_0=O(|\zeta|^{-1})$ by \eqref{eq:conformal-coefficients}. By \eqref{eq:central-domain} and the algebraic coordinate \eqref{eq:central-matrix-coordinate}, the $\zeta$-derivatives of order $k=1,2$ of $\ell$ and $U$ are $O(|\zeta|^{\beta\nu-k})$. Hence we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residual-center}
 |T|_0\leqslant C\rho\,\bigl(|\partial^2\ell|_0+|da_\zeta|_0|d\ell|_0+|d\ell|_0^2+|d\Phi|_0^2\bigr)=O(|\zeta|^{-2+\beta\nu}).
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 3: two harmonic contractions.} In $\zeta=u+iv$, since $\operatorname{tr}_0T=0$ and $\operatorname{div}_0T=0$, we have
\[
 T=A(du^2-dv^2)+2B\,du\,dv,\qquad \partial_uA+\partial_vB=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad \partial_uB-\partial_vA=0.
\]
With  $X_\zeta:=u\partial_u+v\partial_v$ and $Y_\zeta:=-v\partial_u+u\partial_v$,  the functions $P_\zeta:=T(X_\zeta,X_\zeta)$ and $Q_\zeta:=T(X_\zeta,Y_\zeta)$ satisfy $dP_\zeta=*dQ_\zeta$, with $*du=dv$, so they are conjugate harmonic functions on $\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$. By \eqref{eq:residual-center}, $|P_\zeta|+|Q_\zeta|\leqslant2|\zeta|^2|T|_0=O(|\zeta|^{\beta\nu})$, so both extend harmonically across $0$, with $P_\zeta(0)=Q_\zeta(0)=0$, and by \eqref{eq:residual-corner} they are bounded near each $p_c$. On an open arc of $\partial\mathbb D\setminus\{p_c:c\in\mathcal C\}$, $X_\zeta$ and $Y_\zeta$ are the Euclidean unit normal and tangent, and $\zeta$ maps the normal and tangent directions of a rod chart to those of the arc. So $Q_\zeta$ is continuous up to the arc by Step~2, and the first identity of \eqref{eq:residual-boundary} gives $Q_\zeta=0$ there.

 So $Q_\zeta$ is  bounded and harmonic on $\mathbb D$  and vanishes on $\partial\mathbb D$ outside finitely many points, hence $Q_\zeta=0$. Then  $P_\zeta$ is constant, equal to $P_\zeta(0)=0$, and, as $X_\zeta$ and $Y_\zeta$  span away from $0$  and $T$ is trace-free, $T=0$ on  $\Omega\setminus\{o\}$.

Finally, since $T=0$, the second identity in \eqref{eq:residual-boundary} gives $\partial_x\bar a=0$ on $\{x=0\}$, and in a rod chart $\gamma_\beta=e^{2c_\gamma}(dx^2+dy^2)$, so $n=\pm e^{-c_\gamma}\partial_x$. By \eqref{eq:conformal-coefficients}, $\bar a=a+c_\gamma$, and $c_\gamma$ is even across $x=0$ because $\gamma_1$ is even across the rods (Section~\ref{sec:common-coordinates}). Hence $\partial_na=0$.

label: cor:fixed-set-regularity
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:fixed-set-regularity}
Let $(\beta,q)\in J\times\mathcal U_0$ satisfy $\mathcal E(\beta,q)=0$. Then $g_{\beta,q}$ extends smoothly across $\pi^{-1}(\partial\Omega)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We treat a corner. By Proposition~\ref{prop:recovery}, $\partial_x\widehat a=0$ on $\{x=0\}$ and $\partial_y\widehat a=0$ on $\{y=0\}$, so the even extension of $\widehat a$ lies in $C^{2,\alpha}$: its second derivatives are the even extensions of $\partial_x^2\widehat a$ and $\partial_y^2\widehat a$ and the odd extension in each variable of $\partial_x\partial_y\widehat a$, which vanishes on both axes since $\partial_x\widehat a$ and $\partial_y\widehat a$ do. All further estimates are interior Schauder estimates \cite[Theorem~6.2]{GT01} for \eqref{cmp:nonlinear-first-residuals} with zero left-hand sides, after the lifts of Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(b) or even reflection.

We prove that the even extensions of $\widehat\ell,\widehat s,\widehat a$ and the odd extension of $\widehat\omega$ are smooth by induction on $k$. Assume $\widehat\ell,\widehat s,\widehat a\in C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}$ and $\widehat\omega\in C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}$, initially with $k=2$, so that $A_\Phi\in C^{k-1,\alpha}$ by \eqref{eq:connection-regularity}. We improve the regularities of the components in this order:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $D_2\widehat\ell=-|d\widehat\ell|_0^2-6e^{2\widehat a}\in C^{k-1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}$, and the lift $\mathcal L_2$ gives $\widehat\ell\in C^{k+1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}$,
\item by (1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(a), the divided derivatives $x^{-1}\partial_x\widehat\ell$ and $y^{-1}\partial_y\widehat\ell$ in the $D_1$-equation lie in $C^{k-1,\alpha}$, and the lift $\mathcal L_1$ gives $\widehat s\in C^{k+1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}$,
\item $D_\perp\widehat\omega=-e^{\widehat s}\langle d\widehat\ell-2d\widehat s,A_\Phi\rangle_0\in C^{k-1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}$, by \eqref{eq:connection-regularity}, since $\Delta\mathcal L_\perp\widehat\omega=\mathcal L_\perp(D_\perp\widehat\omega)$, the angular lift gives $\widehat\omega\in C^{k+1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}$, and
\item the right-hand side of the equation for $\widehat a$ now lies in $C^{k-1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}$, and even reflection gives $\widehat a\in C^{k+1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}$.
\end{enumerate}
 By the regularized form of the smoothness criterion at the end of Section~\ref{sec:smoothness}, these parities and the angle equalities \eqref{eq:angle-equalities}, which hold by  Lemma~\ref{lem:regularized-chart}, give the smooth extension of $g$.

label: lem:cone-Schauder
title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:central-quantitative-input}, $\rho$ and $\Phi$ are Lipschitz for $\gamma_\beta$, so they have limits $\rho(o)\geqslant M^{-1}$ and $\Phi(o)$ at $o$, and $\Phi(o)=\Phi_o$ by the symmetries, as in \eqref{eq:central-torus-metric}. Hence $\rho$, $a$ and $U$ are bounded, and Lemma~\ref{lem:central-modes} and Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-Schauder} apply to $\rho$, $a$ and $U$.

Applying the constant projection $\Pi_{\Phi_o}$ to the second equation of \eqref{eq:matrix-reduced}, with $\tau_\gamma(\Phi)$ given by \eqref{eq:matrix-tension}, gives the central system:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:central-matrix-system}
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta_\gamma\rho&=-6e^{2a}\rho,\\
 \Delta_\gamma U&=-\langle d\ell,dU\rangle_\gamma+|d\Phi|_\gamma^2U,\\
 \Delta_\gamma a&=\tfrac14\bigl(|d\ell|_\gamma^2-|d\Phi|_\gamma^2\bigr),\qquad\text{with }\gamma=\gamma_\beta.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}


\emph{Step 1: first-order bounds.} Integrating \eqref{eq:central-quantitative-input} along radial segments yields
\[
\begin{gathered}
 |\rho-\rho(o)|\leqslant MR/\sqrt3,\qquad d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi_o)\leqslant MR/\sqrt3,\\
 |U|_o=\sinh d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi_o)\leqslant C(M,R_0)R,\qquad\text{and}\qquad |dU|_\gamma\leqslant C(M,R_0)|d\Phi|_\gamma.
\end{gathered}
\]
Thus the right-hand sides of \eqref{eq:central-matrix-system} are bounded in $L^\infty$ by \eqref{eq:central-quantitative-input}. Interior $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity and estimates for weak solutions with bounded right-hand sides, from the $W^{2,p}$ estimate \cite[Theorem~9.11]{GT01} with $p>\frac{2}{1-\alpha}$ and the Sobolev embedding, on rescaled annuli, turn these $L^\infty$ bounds into the conical bounds
\[
 \|\rho-\rho(o)\|_{RC^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}}+\|U\|_{RC^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}}+\|a\|_{C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}}\leqslant C(I,M,R_0,\alpha)
\]
on $\{R<\frac{3}{4}R_0\}$. Hence the three right-hand sides of \eqref{eq:central-matrix-system} are bounded in $C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$.

\emph{Step 2: weight $2$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:central-modes}, $\rho$, $a$ and $U$ are $\pi$-periodic in $\theta$,  every allowed nonconstant harmonic degree is at least $\frac{2}{\beta}>2$, and $U$ has no constant mode. Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-Schauder} applies at weight $2$, with the uniform gap $\frac{2}{\beta}-2\geqslant\frac{2}{\beta_I}-2>0$, and gives $\rho-\rho(o),\ a-a(o),\ U\in R^2C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, with bounds depending only on $I$, $M$, $R_0$ and $\alpha$.

\emph{Step 3: removing the quadratic term.} Only the $\rho$-equation has nonzero forcing at the center, so we subtract its radial quadratic solution before improving the weight. Since $\Delta_{\gamma_\beta}R^2=12$, the first equation of \eqref{eq:central-matrix-system} gives
\[
 \Delta_{\gamma_\beta}\bigl(\rho-\rho(o)+\tfrac12e^{2a(o)}\rho(o)R^2\bigr)=-6\bigl(e^{2a}\rho-e^{2a(o)}\rho(o)\bigr).
\]
By Step~2 and the product estimates \eqref{eq:weighted-product}, this right-hand side and those of the equations of \eqref{eq:central-matrix-system} for $a-a(o)$ and $U$ lie in $R^2C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$. So \eqref{eq:cone-schauder} at weight $2+\varepsilon$, allowed since $2+\varepsilon<\min\{4,\frac{2}{\beta}\}$, puts the three remainders of \eqref{eq:center-refined} in $R^{2+\varepsilon}C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, and iterating \eqref{eq:annular-estimate} at weight $2+\varepsilon$ on \eqref{eq:central-matrix-system} puts them in $R^{2+\varepsilon}C^{j,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$ for every $j$, which is \eqref{eq:center-refined}.

Since $\frac{2}{\beta}-(2+\varepsilon)\geqslant\frac{2}{\beta_I}-2-\varepsilon>0$ for $\beta\in I$, the constants of Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-Schauder} depend only on $I$ and $\varepsilon$, which gives the bounds on the remainders. Next, \eqref{eq:center-regularity} follows from \eqref{eq:center-refined} and these bounds. Indeed, $R^{2+\varepsilon}\leqslant R_0^{\varepsilon}R^2$ gives $g-g^0=O_{\mathrm b}(R^2)$, with bounds depending only on $I$, $M$, $R_0$ and $\alpha$. As the vector fields $R\partial_R$ and $\partial_\theta$ have $g^0$-length comparable to $R$, this means
\[
 |\nabla_{g^0}^j(g-g^0)|_{g^0}\leqslant CR^{2-j}\qquad\text{for }j=0,1,2,
\]
and, with $\operatorname{Rm}(g^0)=0$ and the comparison of $g$ with $g^0$ below, these bounds give $|\operatorname{Rm}(g)|_g\leqslant C$. The comparison of $g$ with $g^0$ follows from \eqref{eq:central-quantitative-input}, which gives $|a-a(o)|\leqslant2M$, $M^{-2}\leqslant\rho/\rho(o)\leqslant M^2$ and $e^{-d}\Phi_o\leqslant\Phi\leqslant e^d\Phi_o$ for $d:=d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi_o)\leqslant MR_0/\sqrt3$. Finally, $4K_h=|d\Phi|_h^2-|d\log\rho|_h^2$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:reduced}, and \eqref{eq:center-refined} gives $|d\Phi|_h^2=O_{\mathrm b}(R^{2+2\varepsilon})$ and $|d\log\rho|_h^2=O_{\mathrm b}(R^2)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\beta=1$, this is the classical Lichnerowicz-Obata theorem \cite{Oba62}. Let $\beta<1$. Corollary~\ref{cor:fixed-set-regularity} gives smoothness away from $\Sigma$, and \eqref{eq:center-regularity} shows that we satisfy the assumptions of \cite[Definition~1.2]{Mon18}, so \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Mon18} gives \eqref{eq:spectral-inequality}. If we had equality, the stratified Obata theorem \cite[Theorem~3.1]{Mon18} would give
\[
 g=dt^2+\sin^2t\,\bar g,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{\bar g}=2\bar g,
\]
hence $\sec_g=1$ away from $\Sigma$, since the three-dimensional Einstein metric $\bar g$ has constant curvature. But the surfaces $\{\boldsymbol\phi=\phi_0\}$, $\phi_0\in\{0,\pi\}^2$, are fixed by the isometry $\mathsf c$, hence totally geodesic, and they are orthogonal to the torus orbits by \eqref{eq:matrix-ansatz}. So $\pi$ maps them isometrically onto $(\Omega\setminus\{o\},h)$, and $\sec_g=K_h$ on them, while $K_h$ tends to $0$ at $o$ by \eqref{eq:center-regularity}.

label: cmp:kernel-nonnegative
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $q=(f,\xi,b)\in\ker L$, and put $u:=2b-f=\eta-2f$. With $\langle f\rangle_\mu:=\mu(\Omega)^{-1}\int_\Omega f\,d\mu$, $f_0:=f-\langle f\rangle_\mu$, $\|v\|_\mu^2:=\int_\Omega|v|^2\,d\mu$ and
\[
 \mathcal Q_\Phi(\xi):=\int_\Omega\Bigl[|\nabla\xi|_h^2
       +\sum_j|\xi\wedge d\Phi(e_j)|^2\Bigr]d\mu,
\]
where $|\xi\wedge V|^2:=|\xi|^2|V|^2-\langle\xi,V\rangle^2$ and $(e_j)$ is $h$-orthonormal, we prove the identity
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:kernel-nonnegative}
 0=3\bigl(\|df_0\|_\mu^2-4\|f_0\|_\mu^2\bigr)
       +6\|\eta-2f_0\|_\mu^2+\mathcal Q_\Phi(\xi)
       +12\mu(\Omega)\langle f\rangle_\mu^{\,2}.
\end{equation}
All its terms are nonnegative, the first one by Proposition~\ref{prop:spectrum}. The test $(2b-3f,-\xi,-2f)$ below turns the mixed second-order terms into divergences, and, together with the mean identity \eqref{cmp:kernel-mean}, it leaves the scalar spectral form, a square controlling the relative scale $u$, and the harmonic-map form $\mathcal Q_\Phi(\xi)$.

\emph{Two identities.} By \eqref{eq:conic-boundary} and \eqref{eq:corner-domain}, $u$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:kernel-angle}
 u+\xi_s=0\quad\text{on }\{x=0\},\qquad\text{and}\qquad u-\xi_s=0\quad\text{on }\{y=0\}.
\end{equation}
Write $L^\mu_iq:=e^{-2a}L_iq$ and $\Delta_\mu:=\operatorname{div}_\mu\nabla_h$, where $\operatorname{div}_\mu B:=\rho^{-1}\operatorname{div}_h(\rho B)$, with the pullback connection for target-valued $B$. Then \eqref{eq:interior-linear} reads
\[
\begin{aligned}
 L^\mu_1q&=\Delta_\mu f+\langle d\ell,df\rangle_h+12b,\\ L^\mu_2q&=e^{-2a}L_\Phi\xi+d\Phi(\nabla_hf),\\
 L^\mu_3q&=\Delta_\mu b-\langle d\ell,db\rangle_h-\tfrac12\langle d\ell,df\rangle_h+\tfrac12\langle d\Phi,\nabla\xi\rangle_h.
\end{aligned}
\]
The reduced equations \eqref{eq:matrix-reduced} give $\operatorname{div}_\mu\nabla_h\ell=-6$ and $\operatorname{div}_\mu d\Phi=0$, hence $\operatorname{div}_\mu\langle\xi,d\Phi\rangle^\sharp=\langle\nabla\xi,d\Phi\rangle_h$. Since $\langle\xi,R^{\mathbb H^2}(\xi,V)V\rangle=-|\xi\wedge V|^2$, we also have
\[
 -\langle\xi,e^{-2a}L_\Phi\xi\rangle=|\nabla\xi|_h^2+\sum_j|\xi\wedge d\Phi(e_j)|^2-\operatorname{div}_\mu\langle\xi,\nabla\xi\rangle^\sharp.
\]
Define the vector fields
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:kernel-mean-flux}
 W^\flat:=d(f+b)-\tfrac u2\,d\ell+\tfrac12\langle\xi,d\Phi\rangle,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 V:=u\nabla_hf-2fW-\langle\xi,\nabla\xi\rangle^\sharp.
\end{equation}
We use two combinations of the equations $L^\mu_iq=0$: the sum
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:kernel-mean}
 L^\mu_1q+L^\mu_3q=\operatorname{div}_\mu W+3\eta,
\end{equation}
and their pairing with the test $(2b-3f,-\xi,-2f)$, which satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:kernel-test}
 (2b-3f)L^\mu_1q-\langle\xi,L^\mu_2q\rangle-2fL^\mu_3q
 =3|df|_h^2-12f^2+6u^2+|\nabla\xi|_h^2+\sum_j|\xi\wedge d\Phi(e_j)|^2+\operatorname{div}_\mu V.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}_\mu\nabla_h\ell=-6$, $\operatorname{div}_\mu\langle\xi,d\Phi\rangle^\sharp=\langle\nabla\xi,d\Phi\rangle_h$, $du=2\,db-df$ and $12b-3u=3\eta$ give \eqref{cmp:kernel-mean}. For \eqref{cmp:kernel-test}, write $2b-3f=u-2f$ and $-2fL^\mu_3q=-2f(L^\mu_1q+L^\mu_3q)+2fL^\mu_1q$, and use \eqref{cmp:kernel-mean}, $\operatorname{div}_\mu(fW)=\langle df,W^\flat\rangle_h+f\operatorname{div}_\mu W$ and the identity for $L_\Phi$ above. The remaining terms are divergences or cancel by the two algebraic identities
\[
 2W^\flat-du+u\,d\ell-\langle\xi,d\Phi\rangle=3\,df\qquad\text{and}\qquad 12ub-6f\eta=6u^2-12f^2.
\]

\emph{Regularity at rods and corners.} At a corner, $d\ell=\frac{dx}x+\frac{dy}y+d\widehat\ell$ and, in the frame \eqref{eq:target-rod-frame}, $\langle\xi,d\Phi\rangle=\xi_s\,ds+\xi_\perp A_\Phi$ with $ds=-\frac{dx}x+\frac{dy}y+d\widehat s$. Hence we have
\[
 W^\flat=d(f+b)-\tfrac u2\,d\widehat\ell+\tfrac12\xi_s\,d\widehat s+\tfrac12\xi_\perp A_\Phi-\frac{u+\xi_s}{2x}\,dx-\frac{u-\xi_s}{2y}\,dy,
\]
and \eqref{cmp:kernel-angle} with Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(a) makes the last two coefficients $C^{1,\alpha}$, while the other terms are $C^{1,\alpha}$ by the local norms \eqref{eq:side-domain-norm}, \eqref{eq:corner-domain} and the smoothness of the regularized background. At a rod, where $d\ell=\frac{dx}x+d\bar\ell$ and $ds=-\frac{dx}x+d\bar s$, the same holds without the singular term $-\frac{u-\xi_s}{2y}\,dy$. So $W$ and $V$ are $C^{1,\alpha}$ up to the rods and corners, the latter since $\langle\xi,\nabla\xi\rangle=\xi_s\,d\xi_s+\xi_\perp\,d\xi_\perp$ in the orthonormal frame. Consequently $\rho W$ and $\rho V$ vanish on $\partial\Omega$.

\emph{Integration by parts.} Integrate \eqref{cmp:kernel-mean} and \eqref{cmp:kernel-test}, whose left-hand sides vanish, against $d\mu=\rho\,dA_h$ on $\Omega\setminus\{R<\varepsilon\}$. Since $\operatorname{div}_\mu W=\rho^{-1}\operatorname{div}_h(\rho W)$, similarly for $V$, and $\rho W$ and $\rho V$ are $C^{1,\alpha}$ and vanish on $\partial\Omega$, the divergence theorem leaves only the integrals of $\rho\,W\cdot n$ and $\rho\,V\cdot n$ over $\{R=\varepsilon\}$. There, \eqref{eq:central-domain} and \eqref{eq:background-central} give $|W|_h+|V|_h=O(\varepsilon^{\nu-1})$, on a circle of length $O(\varepsilon)$, so these integrals are $O(\varepsilon^\nu)$, and consequently, letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:kernel-energy}
 \int_\Omega\eta\,d\mu=0,\qquad\text{ and }\qquad
 0=3\|df\|_\mu^2-12\|f\|_\mu^2
      +6\|u\|_\mu^2+\mathcal Q_\Phi(\xi).
\end{equation}
Since $\int_\Omega\eta\,d\mu=0$ and $\int_\Omega f_0\,d\mu=0$, writing $u=(\eta-2f_0)-2\langle f\rangle_\mu$ and $f=f_0+\langle f\rangle_\mu$ turns \eqref{cmp:kernel-energy} into \eqref{cmp:kernel-nonnegative}.

The torus-invariant lift of $f_0$ belongs to $H^1(M,g)$, has zero mean and satisfies
\[
 \int_M(|df_0|_g^2-4f_0^2)\,dV_g
     =4\pi^2\bigl(\|df_0\|_\mu^2-4\|f_0\|_\mu^2\bigr).
\]
So every term of \eqref{cmp:kernel-nonnegative} vanishes. Proposition~\ref{prop:spectrum} gives $f_0=0$, the last term gives $\langle f\rangle_\mu=0$, hence $f=0$, and the second term gives $\eta=0$, hence $b=0$. Finally, $\mathcal Q_\Phi(\xi)=0$ gives $\nabla\xi=0$, hence $\xi=0$, since $\xi(o)=0$ by \eqref{eq:central-domain}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:shifted-regularity}
Let $F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)\in\mathcal Y$. The weak solutions of $A_1f=F_1$, $A_2\xi=F_2$ and $A_3b=F_3$, with $b|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, have the regularity and symmetries required for the components of $\mathcal X$ in \eqref{eq:deformation-domain},  with the following componentwise estimates:
\[
 \|f\|_{\mathcal X}\leqslant C\|F_1\|_{\mathcal Y},\qquad
 \|\xi\|_{\mathcal X}\leqslant C\|F_2\|_{\mathcal Y},\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \|b\|_{\mathcal X}\leqslant C\|F_3\|_{\mathcal Y}.
\] Here the $\mathcal X$- and $\mathcal Y$ -norms denote the sums of the local norms involving the indicated component, without the coupled angle conditions.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $u$ for $f$, $\xi$ or $b$, and $F_i$ for the corresponding right-hand side. Each step below gives an estimate of $u$ on a smaller chart by the norm of $F_i$ in $\mathcal Y$, $\mathfrak a_i(u,u)^{1/2}$ and the norm of $u$ in $\mathscr H_i$.

\emph{The center.} By \eqref{eq:center-regularity}, respectively \eqref{eq:seed-bounds} at $g_1$, in the fixed trivialization $\xi^o$, each $A_i$ has the form
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:center-operator}
 A_i=\Delta_\gamma\operatorname{Id}+C_1^a\partial_a+C_0,
 \qquad\text{with}\qquad |C_1|_\gamma=O_{\mathrm b}(R)\quad\text{and}\quad C_0=O_{\mathrm b}(1).
\end{equation}
The finite-energy bound and $F_i\in\mathscr H_i$ give $\Delta_\gamma u\in L^2$. Lemma~\ref{lem:B-cutoffs} extends this weak equation over $o$, and averaging over $\mathcal G$ removes the symmetry restriction on the test functions, since $u$ and $F$ have the symmetries (the averaging argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(c)). In the coordinates $(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta)$, $\Delta_\gamma$ is a uniformly elliptic divergence-form operator with bounded coefficients, so the $L^\infty$ estimate of \cite[Theorem~8.17]{GT01}, applied componentwise, with the coupling terms treated as right-hand sides, gives $u\in L^\infty$. Then \eqref{eq:annular-estimate} with $\delta=0$ gives $u\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, so $C_1^a\partial_au+C_0u\in C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}\subset R^{\nu-2}C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, and \eqref{eq:cone-schauder}, applied to $\Delta_\gamma u=F_i-C_1^a\partial_au-C_0u$, gives $u-u(o)\in R^\nu C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, which is \eqref{eq:central-domain}. Indeed,  the weight is below every allowed nonconstant degree,  by Remark~\ref{rem:weight-restrictions}(3), and $\xi^o_0=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:central-modes}.

\emph{The scalar equations at rods and corners.} At a corner, we have
\[
 e^{2c_\gamma}A_1f
 =D_2f+2\langle d\widehat\ell,df\rangle_0-e^{2c_\gamma}f.
\]
The lift $\mathcal L_2$ of Section~\ref{subsec:division-lifts} and Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts} turn this into an ordinary weak elliptic equation with smooth coefficients on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$. Interior regularity and Schauder estimates \cite[Theorem~8.8, Lemma~9.16 and Theorems~9.19 and~6.2]{GT01} give the required even $C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity. For $A_3$, ordinary boundary Schauder estimates apply along the open rods. At the corners, the zero boundary values and $F_3(c)=0$ are exactly the hypotheses of the Grisvard estimate in Lemma~\ref{lem:grisvard}.

\emph{The equation for $\xi$ at rods and corners.} 
Lemma~\ref{lem:lifted-target} gives the even, respectively odd, $C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity of $\xi_s$ and $\xi_\perp$ at rods and corners, with the associated estimate.

A finite covering of $\Omega$,
the energy estimate, the bound $\|u\|_{\mathscr H_i}^2\leqslant C\mathfrak a_i(u,u)$ and the bound $\|F_i\|_{\mathscr H_i}\leqslant C\|F_i\|_{\mathcal Y}$ checked above give the asserted estimates.

label: eq:curvature-identities
title: Proof
body_md:
Define a $\Phi^*T\mathbb H^2$-valued symmetric $2$-tensor as follows
\[
 \mathcal D:=\rho^{-1}\operatorname{Sym}\nabla(\rho\,d\Phi),
 \qquad\text{so that}\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}_h\mathcal D
 =\tau_h\Phi+d\Phi(\nabla_h\ell)=0.
\]
 We first prove the identity
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:curvature-identities}
 \Delta_gK_h+2\langle d\ell,dK_h\rangle_h=\tfrac12|\mathcal D|_h^2+3(K_h-1)(K_h+3)+\tfrac34\det\nolimits_hB,
\end{equation}
where $\det_hB=\det(h^{-1}B)\geqslant0$.
The Bochner formula for the drift Laplacian $\Delta_g=\Delta_h+\langle d\ell,d\,\cdot\,\rangle_h$ of \eqref{eq:geometric-laplacian}, applied to $\ell$, and the Eells-Sampson Bochner formula \cite{ES64} for $\Phi$, whose tension field is $\tau_h\Phi=-d\Phi(\nabla_h\ell)$ and whose target has curvature $-1$, give (see \cite[(2.2) to (2.4)]{CZ17} for the drift terms)
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bochner-pair}
\begin{aligned}
 \tfrac12\Delta_g|d\ell|^2&=|\operatorname{Hess}_h\ell|^2+K_h|d\ell|^2-\operatorname{Hess}_h\ell(\nabla_h\ell,\nabla_h\ell),\\
 \tfrac12\Delta_g|d\Phi|^2&=|\nabla d\Phi|^2+K_h|d\Phi|^2-\langle\operatorname{Hess}_h\ell,B\rangle+|d\Phi|^4-|B|^2,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where we used $\Delta_h\ell=-6-|d\ell|^2$ and all norms are taken with respect to $h$. In \eqref{eq:bochner-pair}, we substitute  \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities} and the identity $|d\Phi|^4-|B|^2=2\det_hB$, valid for a symmetric form $B$ on a surface.
The definition of $\mathcal D$ gives by expanding
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\mathcal D|^2
 &=|\nabla d\Phi|^2+\langle d\ell,d|d\Phi|^2\rangle\\
 &\quad+\tfrac12\bigl(|d\ell|^2|d\Phi|^2+
                   B(\nabla_h\ell,\nabla_h\ell)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting the two Bochner identities \eqref{eq:bochner-pair} and using
$d|d\Phi|^2=d|d\ell|^2+4\,dK_h$ therefore gives
\eqref{eq:curvature-identities}.

\emph{The bound $K_h\leqslant1$.}  Put $F:=\rho(1-K_h)$. Multiplying $1-K_h$ by $\rho$ gives zero boundary values at the rods and corners and absorbs the extra drift term into the zeroth-order coefficient. Since $\Delta_g\rho=(|d\ell|_h^2-6)\rho$, by \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities} and \eqref{eq:geometric-laplacian}, the identity \eqref{eq:curvature-identities} and $4K_h=|d\Phi|_h^2-|d\ell|_h^2$ give
\[
 \Bigl[\Delta_g-\Bigl(3+\tfrac14|d\ell|_h^2+\tfrac34|d\Phi|_h^2\Bigr)\Bigr]F=-\tfrac\rho2|\mathcal D|_h^2-\tfrac{3\rho}4\det\nolimits_hB\leqslant0.
\]
The  smooth rod and corner models make $K_h$  bounded up to $\partial\Omega$, so $F$ extends continuously by $0$ to $\partial\Omega$. Moreover $F(o)=\rho(o)>0$, since $K_h(o)=0$, by \eqref{eq:center-regularity} in class (C1), and by \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities} and $d\ell(o)=d\Phi(o)=0$ in class (C2). A negative minimum of $F$ would therefore lie in $\Omega\setminus\{o\}$, where the left-hand side would be positive. Hence $F\geqslant0$, that is, $K_h\leqslant1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The identity in \eqref{eq:concavity} is the Hessian formula in \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities}, since $\frac{\operatorname{Hess}_h\sqrt\psi}{\sqrt\psi}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Hess}_h\ell+\frac{1}{4}d\ell\otimes d\ell$, and the inequality follows from $K_h\leqslant1$ and $B\geqslant0$.
\medskip

\noindent\emph{Critical points.} At a critical point $p\neq o$, \eqref{eq:concavity} gives $\operatorname{Hess}_h\psi=2\sqrt\psi\,\operatorname{Hess}_h\sqrt\psi\leqslant-2\psi h$, so $p$ is a nondegenerate local maximum. When $o$ is conic, \eqref{eq:center-refined} gives $\psi=1-\frac{1}{2}e^{2a(o)}R^2+O_{\mathrm b}(R^{2+\varepsilon})$, so that $\partial_R\psi<0$ for small $R>0$. When $o$ is smooth, $K_h(o)=0$ and $\operatorname{Hess}_h\psi(o)=-3h(o)$ by \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities}. In both cases, $o$ is a strict local maximum, and the superlevel sets of $\psi$ near $o$ are disks.
\medskip

\noindent
\emph{Superlevel sets are disks.} Since $\psi>0$ on $\Omega$ and $\psi$ vanishes continuously on $\partial\Omega$, every superlevel set $\{\psi\geqslant t\}$, $t>0$, is compact. As all critical points are local maxima, decreasing $t$ only adds disjoint disks, one at each critical point, and never merges two components \cite[Theorems~3.1 and~3.2]{Mil63}. If $\psi$ had a critical point $p\neq o$, then $o$ and $p$ would lie in distinct components of $\{\psi\geqslant t\}$ for $t$ below $\min\{\psi(o),\psi(p)\}$, hence for every smaller $t>0$. This is impossible for $t$ below the positive minimum of $\psi$ on a path joining $o$ to $p$ in $\Omega$. Hence $o$ is the only critical point of $\psi$, $\max\psi=\psi(o)=1$, and every $E_t$, $0<t<1$, is a closed disk with smooth boundary $\{\psi=t\}$.
\medskip

\noindent
\emph{The level set flow.} On the open set where $d\psi\neq0$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:level-flow}
 \mathsf w:=|d\psi|_h^2,\qquad V_\psi:=\frac{\nabla_h\psi}{\mathsf w},\qquad\text{and}\qquad n:=\frac{\nabla_h\psi}{\sqrt{\mathsf w}}.
\end{equation}
Along a trajectory $\gamma$ of $V_\psi$, parametrized so that $\psi(\gamma(t))=t$, write $\mathsf w(t)$ for $\mathsf w(\gamma(t))$. As $o$ is the only critical point and the superlevel sets are compact, $\gamma$ is defined for $0<t<1$ and converges to $o$, the only point where $\psi=1$, as $t\to1$. For a unit tangent $T$ to the level sets, $\operatorname{Hess}_h\psi=2\sqrt\psi\,\operatorname{Hess}_h\sqrt\psi+\frac{1}{2\psi}d\psi\otimes d\psi$, \eqref{eq:concavity} and $\Delta_h\psi=-6\psi$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:level-flow-derivative}
 \operatorname{Hess}_h\psi(T,T)\leqslant-2t,\qquad\text{and}\qquad -8t\leqslant\frac{d\mathsf w}{dt}=2\operatorname{Hess}_h\psi(n,n)\leqslant\frac{\mathsf w}t-4t.
\end{equation}
\medskip

\noindent
\emph{Gradient bounds and distances.} By the expansions at $o$ in the paragraph on critical points, $\mathsf w(t)\to0$ as $t\to1$, and integrating \eqref{eq:level-flow-derivative} from $t$ to $1$ gives $4t(1-t)\leqslant\mathsf w\leqslant4(1-t^2)$. Since $|\gamma'|_h=\mathsf w^{-1/2}$, the length of $\gamma $ between the level sets $\{\psi=t_1\}$ and $\{\psi=t_2\}$, $t_1<t_2$, is at most
\[
 \int_{t_1}^{t_2}\frac{d\tau}{2\sqrt{\tau(1-\tau)}}=\arcsin\sqrt{t_2}-\arcsin\sqrt{t_1}.
\]
The trajectories therefore have finite length as $t\to0$ and as $t\to1$, and, by continuity of $\psi$, their endpoints lie on $\partial\Omega$ and at $o$. This proves \eqref{eq:base-radius} and the bounds extend to $q\in\partial\Omega$ by continuity. Finally, $|d\psi|_h\leqslant2$ gives the first inequality of \eqref{eq:coord-psi-distance} and the second follows from $d_h(q,\partial\Omega)\leqslant\arcsin\sqrt{\psi(q)}\leqslant\sqrt{2\psi(q)}$ when $\psi(q)\leqslant\frac{1}{2}$ and is immediate if $\psi(q)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}$.

body_md:
\label{lem:scalar}
Let $g$ be in (C1) or (C2). Recall that $0<\psi\leqslant1$ and $\Phi(o)=\Phi_o$. On $\Omega\setminus\{o\}$:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $1-\psi^{-2}\leqslant K_h\leqslant1$ and $|d\Phi|_h\leqslant2\psi^{-1}$,
\item $d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi_o)\leqslant2\operatorname{artanh}\sqrt{1-\psi}$, and
\item $\rho(o)\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-\psi}\bigr)^2\Phi_o\leqslant G\leqslant\rho(o)\bigl(1+\sqrt{1-\psi}\bigr)^2\Phi_o\leqslant4\rho(o)\Phi_o$. In particular, every torus orbit has diameter at most $2\operatorname{diam}(\Sigma)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities}, Lemma~\ref{lem:bochner} and \eqref{eq:base-radius}, we have $4K_h\geqslant-|d\ell|_h^2=-\mathsf w\psi^{-2}\geqslant-4(\psi^{-2}-1)$ and $|d\Phi|_h^2=4K_h+\mathsf w\psi^{-2}\leqslant4\psi^{-2}$, which is (a).

Let $\gamma$ be the trajectory through $q\in\Omega\setminus\{o\}$ of the flow of $V_\psi$ in \eqref{eq:level-flow}, parametrized by $t=\psi$, so that $\gamma(t)\to o$ as $t\to1$. Along $\gamma$, $\bigl|\frac{d}{dt}\Phi(\gamma(t))\bigr|^2\leqslant\frac{|d\Phi|_h^2}{\mathsf w}=\psi^{-2}+\frac{4K_h}{\mathsf w}\leqslant\frac{1}{\psi^2(1-\psi)}$, and since $\Phi\to\Phi_o$ at $o$, we get
\[
 d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi_o)\leqslant\int_\psi^1\frac{dt}{t\sqrt{1-t}}=2\operatorname{artanh}\sqrt{1-\psi},
\]
which is (b).

If $\Phi'\in\mathbb H^2$ lies at distance $D'$ from $\Phi_o$, then $e^{-D'}\Phi_o\leqslant\Phi'\leqslant e^{D'}\Phi_o$, since the eigenvalues of $\Phi_o^{-1/2}\Phi'\,\Phi_o^{-1/2}$ are $e^{\pm D'}$ for the normalization \eqref{eq:intro-matrix-ansatz}. Since $e^{2\operatorname{artanh}\sqrt{1-\psi}}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-\psi}}{1-\sqrt{1-\psi}}$ and $\psi=\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-\psi}\bigr)\bigl(1+\sqrt{1-\psi}\bigr)$, $G=\rho(o)\psi\Phi$ gives (c).

title: Proposition

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:recovery} gives
$\operatorname{Ric}_{g(t)}=3g(t)$, hence $D\operatorname{Ric}_g[\dot g]=3\dot g$ and
$D S_g[\dot g]=0$. The volume variation is $\dot V=\tfrac12\int_M\operatorname{tr}_g\dot g\,dV_g$ while the scalar-curvature variation is
\[
 0=-3\operatorname{tr}_g\dot g+\operatorname{div}_g\Upsilon^\sharp,
 \qquad \text{ with } \qquad \Upsilon:=\operatorname{div}_g\dot g-d\operatorname{tr}_g\dot g.
\]
This is the first-variation identity underlying the Schl\"afli formula
\cite[Theorem~8]{RS00}, see also \cite{RS99}. The cone corollary following \cite[Theorem~9]{RS00} is stated for nonpositive scalar curvature, so we give a direct proof in our setting.

Each $g(t)$ is smooth across $\pi^{-1}(\partial\Omega)$, with rod angles $2\pi$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:fixed-set-regularity}), and $t\mapsto q(t)$ is $C^1$ into $\mathcal X$. Moreover $\partial_n\dot b=0$ on the rods, by Proposition~\ref{prop:recovery} applied to each $q(t)$, so the even extension of $\dot b$ is $C^1$ and $\dot g$ is a $C^1$ tensor across $\pi^{-1}(\partial\Omega)$, and the divergence theorem on $M\setminus\{R<\varepsilon\}$ produces no boundary term at rods and corners.
Only the tube about
$\Sigma$ contributes to the boundary integral.
From \eqref{eq:fixed-cone-identification} and
\eqref{eq:central-domain}, on its boundary $R=\varepsilon$, we have
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Upsilon(\partial_R)=-\frac{2\dot\beta}{\beta R}+O(R^{\nu-1}),\qquad
 n=-\sqrt3e^{-a}\partial_R,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 dA_g=\frac{e^a\beta R}{\sqrt3}(1+O(R^\nu))\,d\theta\,dA_{g|_\Sigma}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Integration over $M\setminus\{R<\varepsilon\}$ gives
\eqref{eq:Schlafli}:
\[
 6\dot V
 =\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{R=\varepsilon}\Upsilon(n)\,dA_g
 =4\pi\dot\beta\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma,g).
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Corollary~\ref{cor:concavity} makes $E_t$ a closed disk with smooth boundary,
and Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar}(a) bounds its curvature: $|K_h|\leqslant t^{-2}$ on $E_t$. Hence $K_h\in L^2(E_t,dA_h)$, and the Riesz representation theorem in $H^1_0(E_t)$, normed by the Dirichlet energy, gives a unique weak solution $\sigma\in H^1_0(E_t)$ of \eqref{eq:core-flattening}. 

The estimate on $\sigma$ comes from barriers based on the conformal metrics $\psi^{\pm1/2}h$. By \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities}, $\Delta_h\log\psi=\psi^{-1}\Delta_h\psi-|d\ell|_h^2=-6-|d\ell|_h^2$ and $4K_h=|d\Phi|_h^2-|d\ell|_h^2$, so we have
\[
 K_h-\tfrac14\Delta_h\log\psi=\tfrac32+\tfrac14|d\Phi|_h^2>0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 K_h+\tfrac14\Delta_h\log\psi\leqslant-\tfrac12:
\]
the metrics $\psi^{1/2}h$ and $\psi^{-1/2}h$ have curvatures of opposite signs. Consequently, as $\Delta_h\sigma=K_h$, the functions $\frac{1}{4}\log(\psi/t)\pm\sigma\in H^1(E_t)$ are weakly superharmonic and vanish on $\partial E_t$. The weak minimum principle \cite[Theorem~8.1]{GT01} gives $\frac{1}{4}\log(\psi/t)\pm\sigma\geqslant0$, which is \eqref{eq:core-flattening-bound}. Near $o$, $\Delta_{\gamma_\beta}\sigma=e^{2a}K_h$ is bounded in $C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$ by \eqref{eq:center-regularity}, and $\sigma$ is invariant, so Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-Schauder} with $\delta=2$ shows that $\sigma$ has a limit $\sigma(o)$ and $\sigma-\sigma(o)\in R^2C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$, and in particular $\sigma$ has no logarithmic term. Thus the conformal change preserves the cone angle, while
$K_{\widetilde h}=e^{-2\sigma}(K_h-\Delta_h\sigma)=0$ away from $o$.
Uniqueness preserves the symmetries.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Flat balls.} Let $0<t<1$, and let $\widetilde h=e^{2\sigma}h$ be the flat metric of Lemma~\ref{lem:flattened-cores} on the core $E_t$, smooth in class (C2), and with one cone point $o$ of angle $2\pi\beta<2\pi$ in class (C1). For $q\in E_t$ in class (C2), and for $q=o$ in class (C1), the $\widetilde h$-exponential map at $q$ is an isometry from the Euclidean disk, respectively the flat cone of angle $2\pi\beta$, of radius $d_{\widetilde h}(q,\partial E_t)$ onto $B_{\widetilde h}(q,d_{\widetilde h}(q,\partial E_t))$. Indeed, $\widetilde h$ has no conjugate points, and a first point in the cut locus would give a flat geodesic bigon in $E_t$, whose two interior angles would sum to $0$ by Gauss-Bonnet.

On the universal cover $\mathbb R^2$ of the torus orbits put $y_a:=\sqrt{\rho(o)}\,\phi_a$.
Then
$g=h+\psi\Phi_{ab}\,dy_ady_b$. This change is only for local estimates
and does not change the generators $X_1,X_2$ of \eqref{eq:matrix-ansatz}, whose flows are $2\pi$-periodic.


\emph{ The conic center.} Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:flattened-cores} on
$E_{1/2}$. Since $|d\psi|_h\leqslant2$, this yields
\[
 |\sigma|\leqslant\tfrac14\log2,\qquad
 d_h(o,\partial E_{1/2})\geqslant\tfrac14,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 d_{\widetilde h}(o,\partial E_{1/2})\geqslant\tfrac14\,2^{-1/4}.
\]
Put $r_0:=\frac{1}{4}\,2^{-1/4}$. The ball $B_{\widetilde h}(o,r_0)$ is a flat cone of angle $2\pi\beta$, by the paragraph on flat balls and $d_{\widetilde h}(o,\partial E_{1/2})\geqslant r_0$. Write there
\[
 \widetilde h=\tfrac13(d\widetilde R^2+\beta^2\widetilde R^2d\theta^2),\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 h=e^{-2\sigma}\widetilde h.
\]
Here $\widetilde R$ is the radius of this local chart, which is a priori distinct from the
prescribed $R$. The central symmetries act by their original rotations and reflections in the chart $(\widetilde R,\theta)$, so the mode restrictions
of Lemma~\ref{lem:central-modes} are unchanged.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:center-expansion} with $(\gamma_\beta,\rho,\Phi,a,R)$ replaced by $(\widetilde h,\psi,\Phi,-\sigma,\widetilde R)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:reduced} verifies (H1), since the reference metric may be changed and $\rho/\psi=\rho(o)$ is constant. On $B_{\widetilde h}(o,r_0)\subset E_{1/2}$, Lemmas~\ref{lem:scalar} and~\ref{lem:flattened-cores} give
\[
 |\sigma|\leqslant\tfrac14\log2,\qquad \tfrac12\leqslant\psi\leqslant1,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 |d\psi|_{\widetilde h}+|d\Phi|_{\widetilde h}\leqslant e^{|\sigma|}\bigl(|d\psi|_h+|d\Phi|_h\bigr)\leqslant6\cdot2^{1/4},
\]
which gives \eqref{eq:central-quantitative-input} with a universal $M$. Lemma~\ref{lem:center-expansion}, with $g^0=e^{-2\sigma(o)}\widetilde h+(\Phi_o)_{ab}\,dy_ady_b$, gives $|\operatorname{Rm}(g)|\leqslant C$ and $C^{-1}g^0\leqslant g\leqslant Cg^0$ on the chart.
Since $C=C(I)$, this chart contains a tube $\{0<d_g(\Sigma,\cdot)<r_*\}$, proving \eqref{eq:curv-central}.

For every $g$ in (C2) and $\delta\in(0,1)$, the core $E_\delta$ admits a normal chart at $o$ and, where needed, a cylinder chart in the coordinates $(t,\Theta)$ of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:core-retraction}, on coordinate domains independent of $g$. title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{ Cores of metrics with a smooth center.} We use the flat balls and the fiber coordinates $y_a:=\sqrt{\rho(o)}\,\phi_a$ of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:curv-central}. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:flattened-cores} on $E_{\delta/2}$. Then, we have
\[
 |\sigma|\leqslant\tfrac14\log(2/\delta),\qquad
 d_h(E_\delta,\partial E_{\delta/2})\geqslant\tfrac\delta4,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 d_{\widetilde h}(E_\delta,\partial E_{\delta/2})
       \geqslant\tfrac\delta4(\delta/2)^{1/4}.
\]
 With $r_\delta:=\frac{\delta}{4}(\frac{\delta}{2})^{1/4}$,  the  flat balls of radius $r_\delta$  about the points of $E_\delta$ are Euclidean disks contained in $E_{\delta/2}$. In such a chart $h=e^{-2\sigma}|dx|^2$, which with the bound for $\sigma$ below gives the metric comparison. label: lem:torus-limit
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{(a)} An arbitrary normalization of the first jets of the limiting Killing fields need not preserve the original integral lattice $2\pi\mathbb Z^2$ of periods. At a corner, the primitive rod fields have unit rotation derivatives in the normal planes, whatever the scale, and this fixes their normalization.

 After a subsequence, the adjacent rod vectors $v_1,v_2$ at $c_i$ are fixed. By the corner model, $V_{a,i}:=(v_a)_1X_{1,i}+(v_a)_2X_{2,i}$ vanishes at $c_i$, and $\nabla V_{1,i}(c_i)$, $\nabla V_{2,i}(c_i)$ are the rotations $J\oplus0$ and $0\oplus J$ of an orthogonal splitting of $T_{c_i}U_i$ into two planes, with $J:=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ in orthonormal bases. As $(v_1,v_2)\in\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb Z)$, the $1$-jets of $X_{1,i},X_{2,i}$ at $c_i$ are therefore bounded and independent, uniformly in $i$, and  \eqref{eq:killing-transport}, with its differentiated form, gives, on each compact subset $Q$ of the converging regions and for $q\in Q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:killing-propagation}
 \|X\|_{C^{j+1}(Q)}\leqslant C_{Q,j}\bigl(|X(q)|+|\nabla X(q)|\bigr).
\end{equation}


 Hence $X_{a,i}\to X_a$ smoothly on compact subsets, and the limits, with $2\pi$-periodic flows and the above $1$-jets at $c$, generate an effective action with the lattice $2\pi\mathbb Z^2$ \cite[proof of Theorem~27]{CLW08}. 

 On each fixed ball about $c$, the center-of-mass construction \cite[Propositions~3.1 and~3.7]{GK73} modifies the convergence embeddings by a $C^\infty$-small amount to embeddings $F_i$ with $(F_i)_*X_a=X_{a,i}$, which intertwine the actions and therefore preserve the stabilizers.

\emph{(b)}  Bases $X'_{1,i},X'_{2,i}$ of the span of $X_{1,i},X_{2,i}$, orthonormal for the inner product of $1$-jets at $p_i$, converge, by \eqref{eq:killing-propagation} with $q=p_i$, to independent commuting Killing vector fields $Y_1,Y_2$ of $g_{\mathcal N}$. 

 By \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Web19}, every Killing vector field of $g_{\mathcal N}$ vanishes somewhere, and the isometries fixing a point form a compact group. So the closures $K_1,K_2$ of the flows of $Y_1,Y_2$ are compact, $\mathbb T':=K_1K_2$ is a torus, and a Killing vector field whose flow is dense in $\mathbb T'$ vanishes at a point $c$, again by \cite{Web19}, which is fixed by $\mathbb T'$.  The commuting skew endomorphisms $\nabla Y_1(c)$ and $\nabla Y_2(c)$ are independent, since a Killing vector field vanishing at $c$ is determined by its derivative there, so in a common orthonormal basis they are $\operatorname{diag}(a_1J,a_2J)$ and $\operatorname{diag}(b_1J,b_2J)$ with $(a_1,a_2)$ and $(b_1,b_2)$ independent. Choose $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ with $\lambda_1a_j+\lambda_2b_j\neq0$ for $j=1,2$, so that $Z:=\lambda_1Y_1+\lambda_2Y_2$ has invertible derivative $\nabla Z(c)$, and put $Z_i:=\lambda_1X'_{1,i}+\lambda_2X'_{2,i}$. As $Z_i\to Z$ smoothly, $Z_i$ vanishes at a point $c_i$, isolated in the vanishing set of $Z_i$, with $c_i\to c$. The torus acting on $U_i$ commutes with $Z_i$, which is a constant combination of its generators, so it preserves the vanishing set of $Z_i$. The orbit of $c_i$ is connected and lies in this set, in which $c_i$ is isolated, so it is $\{c_i\}$: the point $c_i$ is fixed by the torus, that is, a corner.

label: cor:ale-exclusion
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:ale-exclusion}
Let $(\mathcal N,g_{\mathcal N})$ be a complete Ricci-flat four-manifold with finite curvature energy, Euclidean volume growth and an effective isometric action of $\mathbb R^2/2\pi\mathbb Z^2$, whose orbits are principal orbits, rods and corners, and whose primitive rod vectors $v,v'$ satisfy
\[
 |\det(v,v')|=1\qquad\text{whenever }v\neq\pm v'.
\] Then $(\mathcal N,g_{\mathcal N})$ is isometric to the Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Theorem~1.5]{BKN89}, $(\mathcal N,g_{\mathcal N})$ is ALE.

\emph{An invariant cross-section of the end.} The tangent cone $\mathbb R^4/\Gamma$ at infinity alone does not identify the stabilizers, so we construct a  $\mathbb T^2$-invariant cross-section of the end. Let $r$ be  an ALE radius, extended smoothly inside, and let $H$ be the average of $r^2\circ t$ over $t\in\mathbb T^2$, an invariant proper function. Since $\operatorname{Hess} r^2=2g_{\mathcal N}+o(1)$ and $\mathbb T^2$  acts by isometries, $\operatorname{Hess} H=2g_{\mathcal N}+o(1)$, and $|dH|=O(r)$. Along the radial rays of the ALE coordinates,  whose acceleration is $o(r^{-1})$, this gives $\partial_r^2H=2+o(1)$, hence $\partial_rH=2r+o(r)>0$. So the large level sets $Y$ of $H$ are invariant radial graphs over $\mathbb S^3/\Gamma$.

 The action on $Y$ is effective: an element  fixing $Y$ pointwise also fixes  its invariant unit normal, hence is the identity isometry.  Since $\pi_1(Y)\approx\Gamma$ is finite, the orbit space $Y/\mathbb T^2$ is an interval  whose endpoints are circle orbits, with stabilizers generated by the rod vectors  $v_-,v_+$ of the two unbounded rods of $\mathcal N$  \cite[Section~2.5]{OR70}. Thus
\[
 \Gamma\approx\mathbb Z^2/(\mathbb Zv_-+\mathbb Zv_+),\qquad\text{and}\qquad |\Gamma|=|\det(v_-,v_+)|,
\]
 compare \cite[Section~2.2, (2.6)]{CS04}. In the application to blow-ups, the two unbounded rods need not arise from adjacent sides of the orbit space, which is why the hypothesis concerns all pairs of distinct rod vectors. It gives $|\Gamma|=1$, so the asymptotic volume ratio of $g_{\mathcal N}$ is one, and the equality case of the Bishop-Gromov inequality gives $(\mathcal N,g_{\mathcal N})\approx\mathbb R^4$.

\label{prop:curv-bound}
There is $C=C(I,v)$ such that every metric $g=g_{\beta,q}$ as in \eqref{eq:perturbed-metric} with $\mathcal E(\beta,q)=0$, $\beta\in I$ and $\operatorname{Vol}(g)\geqslant v$ satisfies
\[
 \sup_{M\setminus\Sigma}|\operatorname{Rm}(g)|\leqslant C.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, towards a contradiction, that $\Lambda_i=\max|\operatorname{Rm}(g_i)|=|\operatorname{Rm}(g_i)|(p_i)\to+\infty$.
By \eqref{eq:curv-central}, $d_{g_i}(p_i,\Sigma)\geqslant r_*$.
Thus $\Sigma$ escapes after rescaling by $\Lambda_i$: $d_{\Lambda_ig_i}(p_i,\Sigma)\geqslant\Lambda_i^{1/2}r_*\to+\infty$.
Noncollapse \eqref{eq:local-noncollapse} and Einstein compactness \cite[Theorem~2.2 and Section~3]{And89} therefore give
\[
 (M\setminus\Sigma,\Lambda_i g_i,p_i)\longrightarrow(\mathcal N,g_{\mathcal N},p),
 \qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g_{\mathcal N})=0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad |\operatorname{Rm}(g_{\mathcal N})|(p)=1,
\]
where $\mathcal N$ has Euclidean volume growth, by \eqref{eq:local-noncollapse}, and finite curvature energy, by \eqref{eq:curv-energy}. Since $\Sigma$ escapes, Lemma~\ref{lem:torus-limit}(b), applied with $U_i:=M\setminus\Sigma$, gives corners $c_i$ converging to a point $c\in\mathcal N$. Lemma~\ref{lem:torus-limit}(a) then gives an effective isometric action of $\mathbb R^2/2\pi\mathbb Z^2$ on $\mathcal N$, generated by the limits of $X_1,X_2$, and convergence maps on balls about $c$ which preserve the stabilizers. So every orbit of $\mathcal N$ is the image of an orbit of $M\setminus\Sigma$ with the same stabilizer: a principal orbit, a corner, or a rod with one of the rod vectors of Section~\ref{sec:geometry}, which satisfy \eqref{eq:rod-determinant}. Corollary~\ref{cor:ale-exclusion} therefore gives $(\mathcal N,g_{\mathcal N})\approx\mathbb R^4$, which contradicts $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_{\mathcal N})|(p)=1$.

label: lem:coord-conformal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:coord-conformal}
Every metric as in \eqref{eq:coord-assumptions} satisfies
$|a|\leqslant C$ on $\Omega$. Equivalently,
$e^{-2C}\gamma_\beta\leqslant h\leqslant e^{2C}\gamma_\beta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We keep the notation $\gamma_\beta$ for the reflection of $\gamma_\beta$ to the closed reflected surface $\bar S$  just constructed. It is
smooth away from the cone points, because $\gamma_1$ is even across the
rods and at the corners (Section~\ref{sec:common-coordinates}), and $h=e^{2a}\gamma_\beta$ on every copy $S_{\phi_0}$. It remains to bound the solution $a$ of the curvature equation $\Delta_{\gamma_\beta}a=K_{\gamma_\beta}-K_he^{2a}$.

\emph{A negatively curved reference metric.} By Gauss-Bonnet on $\bar S$, with $\chi(\bar S)=4-m$ and four cone points of angle $2\pi\beta$, the following constant is positive:
\[
 c_\beta:=-\frac{\int_{\bar S}K_{\gamma_\beta}\,dA_{\gamma_\beta}}{\operatorname{Area}(\bar S,\gamma_\beta)}=\frac{2\pi(m-4\beta)}{\operatorname{Area}(\bar S,\gamma_\beta)}>0.
\]
Let $v_\beta$ be the solution with $\int_{\bar S}v_\beta\,dA_{\gamma_\beta}=0$ of
\[
 \Delta_{\gamma_\beta}v_\beta=K_{\gamma_\beta}+c_\beta.
\]
For $\beta\in I$, the metrics $\gamma_\beta$ have uniform divergence-form ellipticity in the cone charts and uniform Poincar\'e constants, so the $L^\infty$ estimate of \cite[Theorem~8.17]{GT01} and the normalization $\int_{\bar S}v_\beta\,dA_{\gamma_\beta}=0$ give $\|v_\beta\|_{L^\infty}\leqslant C_I$. The metric $k_\beta:=e^{2v_\beta}\gamma_\beta$ has cone angle $2\pi\beta$ at the four cone points and
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 K_{k_\beta}=e^{-2v_\beta}\bigl(K_{\gamma_\beta}-\Delta_{\gamma_\beta}v_\beta\bigr)=-c_\beta e^{-2v_\beta}\in[-C_I,-c_I],\\
 \text{and}\qquad \operatorname{diam}(\bar S,k_\beta)\geqslant c_I>0\qquad\text{for }\beta\in I.
 \end{gathered}
\]


\emph{Lower bound.} Write $h=e^{2u}k_\beta$, so that $u=a-v_\beta$ and
\[
 \Delta_{k_\beta}u=K_{k_\beta}-K_he^{2u}.
\]
The weak form of this equation holds across the four cone points by Lemma~\ref{lem:B-cutoffs}, since $h$ and $k_\beta$ have the same cone angle there, so that $u$ is continuous with finite energy \cite[Proposition~15]{MW17}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:curv-central}  and Proposition~\ref{prop:curv-bound},
$K_h\geqslant-C_1$.
For a constant $u_0$ with $C_1e^{2u_0}<c_I$, the right-hand side is negative on the open set $\{u<u_0\}$, so $u$ is weakly superharmonic there, with $u=u_0$ on its boundary, and the weak minimum principle \cite[Theorem~8.1]{GT01} makes this set empty. Hence $u\geqslant-C$.

\emph{Diameter.} By \eqref{eq:base-radius}, every point of the closure of a copy $S_{\phi_0}$ is joined to the cone point $o_{\phi_0}:=(o,\phi_0)$ by a path of $h$-length at most $\frac{\pi}{2}$ in that copy. For a corner $c$, the point $\tilde c$ of $S$ over $c$ lies in the closure of all four copies, so every point of $\bar S$ lies at distance at most $\pi$ from $\tilde c$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reflected-diameter}
 \operatorname{diam}(\bar S,h)\leqslant2\pi.
\end{equation}

\emph{Upper bound.}  By the lower bound, $\Delta_hu=e^{-2u}K_{k_\beta}-K_h$ is bounded: $|\Delta_hu|\leqslant C$. Let $p$ be a minimum point of $u$, and put $u_p:=u-u(p)\geqslant0$. Cover $\bar S$ by balls of a fixed radius in two kinds of charts: normal coordinates of $S$ at $h$-distance at least $\frac{1}{2}r_*$ from the cone points, given by \eqref{eq:uniform-geometry}, and the cone charts $(\widetilde R\cos\theta,\widetilde R\sin\theta)$ constructed in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:curv-central}  near them. $\Delta_h$ is uniformly elliptic in both, for $\beta\in I$. By \eqref{eq:reflected-diameter}, every $q\in\bar S$ is joined to $p$ by a chain of at most $C(I,v)$ overlapping such balls. Applied to $u_p$ from ball to ball, starting from $u_p(p)=0$, the Harnack inequality \cite[Theorems~8.17 and~8.18]{GT01} gives $u_p(q)\leqslant C$. 

 $h\geqslant e^{2u(p)}k_\beta$ and \eqref{eq:reflected-diameter} give $e^{u(p)}c_I\leqslant e^{u(p)}\operatorname{diam}(\bar S,k_\beta)\leqslant2\pi$, so $u\leqslant u(p)+C\leqslant C$. Hence $|u|\leqslant C$ and $|a|\leqslant|u|+|v_\beta|\leqslant C$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: bounds in the fixed charts.} By
\eqref{eq:area-volume} and \eqref{eq:local-noncollapse},
$c\leqslant\rho_i(o)\leqslant C$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:coord-conformal}, $e^{-2C}\gamma_{\beta_i}\leqslant h_i\leqslant e^{2C}\gamma_{\beta_i}$.

(i) \emph{Interior.} Let $U$ be a closed interior chart or the central
chart. By \eqref{eq:coord-psi-distance} and Lemma~\ref{lem:coord-conformal},
$\psi_i\geqslant\delta(U)>0$ on $U$. Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar} then bounds
$|d\rho_i|_\gamma$, $|d\Phi_i|_\gamma$ and $d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi_i,\Phi_o)$
on $U$. On interior charts, with Lemma~\ref{lem:coord-conformal}, these are the hypotheses of the regularity improvement \eqref{eq:local-regularity} with $\gamma=\gamma_{\beta_i}$ and $u=a_i$, with constants depending only on $I$, $v$ and $U$. Since $c\leqslant\rho_i(o)\leqslant C$, \eqref{eq:local-regularity}, applied to $(a_i,\psi_i,\Phi_i)$ with $\rho_i=\rho_i(o)\psi_i$, bounds $(\rho_i,\Phi_i,a_i)$ in every $C^k$ on interior charts.

(ii) \emph{Center.} On the central chart, (i) gives (H1) and (H2) of Lemma~\ref{lem:center-expansion} with a uniform constant $M$. Here we use
$|d\rho_i|_\gamma+|d\Phi_i|_\gamma=e^{a_i}(|d\rho_i|_h+|d\Phi_i|_h)$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:center-expansion}, with a fixed $\varepsilon$, therefore gives, uniformly in $i$
and in all $\mathrm b$ derivatives,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coord-central-derivatives}
 a_i-a_i(o),\quad \rho_i-\rho_i(o),\quad
 \Pi_{\Phi_o}\Phi_i=O_{\mathrm b}(R^2),
\end{equation}
with the remainders of \eqref{eq:center-refined} uniformly bounded.

(iii) \emph{Rods and corners.}
We treat a corner $c$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:coord-conformal}, the fixed corner chart, extended by reflection, is a reflected chart \eqref{eq:reflected-chart} of fixed size, in which $h_i=e^{2\widehat a_i}(dx^2+dy^2)$ with $\widehat a_i$ even and $|\widehat a_i|\leqslant C$.

 The Gauss curvature of $h_i$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reflected-curvature-equation}
 \Delta_0\widehat a_i=-K_{h_i}e^{2\widehat a_i}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:uniform-geometry} and \eqref{eq:reflected-facts}, $|\nabla_h^jK_{h_i}|\leqslant C_j$, and successive $W^{2,p}$ and Schauder estimates \cite[Theorems~9.11 and~6.2]{GT01} for \eqref{eq:reflected-curvature-equation} give uniform $C^{j,\alpha}$ bounds for $\widehat a_i$.

 Let $X_v$ and $X_{v'}$ be the Killing fields of the two rod vectors $v$ and $v'$ at $c$, which vanish on $\{x=0\}$ and on $\{y=0\}$ respectively, and let $G$ be the Gram matrix in this basis.  These Killing fields are bounded by Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar}(c), hence in every $C^j$ on balls of fixed radius, since $\nabla^*\nabla X=\operatorname{Ric}(X)=3X$ for each of them, and interior elliptic estimates \cite[Theorems~9.11 and~6.2]{GT01} apply on the balls given by \eqref{eq:uniform-geometry}. By \eqref{eq:reflected-facts} and the bounds for $\widehat a_i$, the entries $G_{ab}$ are bounded in every $C^j$ in the chart $(x,y)$. They are even in each variable, because the reflections of $S$ across the lifts of the two rods at $c$ are the half-turns $\boldsymbol\phi\mapsto\boldsymbol\phi+\pi v$ and $\boldsymbol\phi\mapsto\boldsymbol\phi+\pi v'$, which fix $X_v$ and $X_{v'}$. Since $X_v=0$ on $\{x=0\}$ and $X_{v'}=0$ on $\{y=0\}$, the functions $G_{11},G_{12}$ vanish with their first $x$-derivatives on $\{x=0\}$, and $G_{22},G_{12}$ with their first $y$-derivatives on $\{y=0\}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(a) with $(k,l)=(2,0)$, $(0,2)$ and $(2,2)$, which loses two, two and four derivatives, gives
\[
 G_{11}=x^2H_{11},\qquad G_{22}=y^2H_{22},\qquad G_{12}=x^2y^2H_{12},\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \widehat G_i=\begin{pmatrix}H_{11}&xyH_{12}\\ xyH_{12}&H_{22}\end{pmatrix},
\]
with $H_{ab}$ even and bounded in every $C^j$. This bounds $e^{2\widehat a_i}$ and $\widehat G_i$, which are the coefficients of $g_i$ along $S$ in the Cartesian chart \eqref{eq:cartesian}, by \eqref{eq:reflected-metric}. On an open-rod chart, the same Killing vector field estimates and division by the single normal variable bound $\bar G_i$ in every $C^j$.

  Since $\rho_i=x\sqrt{\det\bar G_i}$ for $x\geqslant0$, the same formula defines a smooth odd extension of $\rho_i$ across an open rod, used in Step~3. The extensions satisfy $\Delta_0\rho_i=-6e^{2\bar a_i}\rho_i$ in a reflected rod chart, by \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities}. They are bounded by $\rho_i(o)\leqslant C$, and the same argument bounds $e^{2\bar a_i}$ in every $C^j$, so interior elliptic estimates bound them in every $C^j$ on a smaller reflected chart, without  a uniform positive lower bound for $\bar G_i$.

\emph{Step 2: convergence of the coefficients.} By Step~1 and the Arzel\`a-Ascoli theorem, a diagonal subsequence of the coefficients converges in every $C^k$ on each closed chart away from $o$: $(\rho_i,\Phi_i,a_i)$ on interior charts, and $\widehat a_i$, $\widehat G_i$, respectively $\bar a_i$, $\bar G_i$ and the odd extensions of $\rho_i$, extended with their parities, on corner, respectively rod, charts. At $o$, $a_i(o)$ and $\rho_i(o)$ converge, and \eqref{eq:coord-central-derivatives} gives uniform convergence across $o$. In particular, $a_i$, $\rho_i$ and the entries of $G_i$ converge uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ in the prescribed charts.

\emph{Step 3: positivity of the limit.} The limits of the positive definite matrices $\widehat G_i$ and $\bar G_i$ are a priori only positive semidefinite, and at a rod $\det\bar G_i=(\rho_i/x)^2$ could tend to zero; Hopf's lemma, applied to the limit of the odd extensions of $\rho_i$, excludes this. On interior charts and on the central chart, $\psi_i\geqslant\delta(U)$, $\rho_i(o)\geqslant c$ (Step~1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar}(c) bound $G_i$ from below by a positive multiple of $\Phi_o$, uniformly in $i$. At a corner $c$, the angle conditions of \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-corner} and the oddness of $\widehat G_{12}$ give $\widehat G_\infty(c)=e^{2\widehat a_\infty(c)}I\geqslant e^{-2C}I$. At an open rod, the limit $\rho_\infty$ of the odd extensions is positive on $\{x>0\}$, by \eqref{eq:coord-psi-distance} and $\rho_i(o)\geqslant c$, and it vanishes on $\{x=0\}$. Since $\Delta_0\rho_\infty\leqslant0$ on $\{x>0\}$, Hopf's lemma \cite[Lemma~3.4]{GT01} gives $\partial_x\rho_\infty>0$ on $\{x=0\}$, so $\det\bar G_\infty=(\rho_\infty/x)^2>0$ up to $\{x=0\}$, with $\rho_\infty/x:=\partial_x\rho_\infty$ on $\{x=0\}$. As a limit of positive definite matrices, $\bar G_\infty$ is positive semidefinite, hence positive definite. So $\widehat G_\infty$ and $\bar G_\infty$ are uniformly positive definite on smaller closed corner and rod charts, and so are $\widehat G_i$ and $\bar G_i$ for large $i$, by uniform convergence.

\emph{Step 4: the limit metric and convergence in $\mathcal X$.} Uniform positivity, the parity and angle conditions \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-side} and \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-corner}, the finite symmetries and $\operatorname{Ric}(g_i)=3g_i$ pass to the limit. So $g_\infty$ is Einstein on $\pi^{-1}(\Omega\setminus\{o\})$, smooth across the rods and corners and invariant under the torus and $\mathcal G$, and its cone angle along $\Sigma$ is $2\pi\beta_*$, since $h_\infty=e^{2a_\infty}\gamma_{\beta_*}$ with $a_\infty$ continuous at $o$. By \eqref{eq:coord-central-derivatives}, it satisfies \eqref{eq:background-central}, hence the assumptions made on $g_*$ in Section~\ref{sec:spaces}. Moreover, by Step~3, the regularized coordinates \eqref{eq:gram-regular-coordinates} of $\widehat G_i$ and $\bar G_i$ converge in every $C^k$, and the inverse map in  Lemma~\ref{lem:regularized-chart} converts this convergence into convergence of the components of $q_i$ in the norms \eqref{eq:side-domain-norm} and \eqref{eq:corner-domain}. On interior charts, it is immediate. At $o$, $f_i(o)$ and $b_i(o)$ tend to $0$, and the remainders $f_i-f_i(o)$, $b_i-b_i(o)$ and $\xi_i^o$ are bounded in $R^2C^{3,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$ by \eqref{eq:coord-central-derivatives} and tend to zero away from $o$. As $\nu<2$, the embedding $R^2C^{3,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}\hookrightarrow R^\nu C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm b}$ is compact \cite[Lemma~2.2]{PR00}, which proves \eqref{eq:coord-deformation-convergence}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\operatorname{Ric}(g)=\lambda g$, with $\lambda>0$.
An orientation-reversing isometry is given by $\mathsf c_1$ of \eqref{eq:group-actions} which extends across the rods and corners. Since $b_2^+(M_k)=k\geqslant 1$, we can choose a nonzero smooth harmonic
self-dual two-form $\omega_+$ on $M_k$.
The torus acts trivially on cohomology, so $\omega_+$ is torus-invariant and $|\omega_+|_g$ is constant on each torus orbit, by uniqueness of the harmonic representative.
The form $\omega_-:=\mathsf c_1^*\omega_+$ is harmonic and anti-self-dual,
and, since $\mathsf c_1$ preserves every torus orbit, we have
\[
 |\omega_-|_g^2=|\omega_+|_g^2.
\]

Define $H_{ij}:=(\omega_+)_i{}^p(\omega_-)_{jp}$ and $(\mathring{\operatorname{Rm}}_gH)_{ij}:=R_{ikjl}H^{kl}$. By \cite[Proposition~2.1, equation~(12)]{Ozu26}, $H$ is trace-free and divergence-free, $|H|_g^2=|\omega_+|_g^2|\omega_-|_g^2=|\omega_+|_g^4$, and, since $\operatorname{Ric}_g=\lambda g$, we have
\[
 \int_{M_k}\bigl\langle\nabla^*\nabla H-2\mathring{\operatorname{Rm}}_gH,H\bigr\rangle_g\,dV_g
 =-2\lambda\int_{M_k}|\omega_+|_g^4\,dV_g-\frac{1}{2}\int_{M_k}\bigl|d(|\omega_+|_g^2)\bigr|_g^2\,dV_g<0.
\]

Thus the smooth tensor $H$, which is trace-free and divergence-free, is a destabilizing direction.

\label{cor:finite-fundamental-groups}
For $k\geqslant1$, the quotients $(Z^{(k)},g_Z^{(k)})$ are closed
oriented Einstein four-manifolds satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{Ric}(g_Z^{(k)})=3g_Z^{(k)},\qquad
 \pi_1(Z^{(k)})=\mathbb Z_{k+1},\qquad
 \chi(Z^{(k)})=\tfrac m2,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \tau(Z^{(k)})=2-\tfrac m2.
\]
Their integral homology groups are
\[
 H_1(Z^{(k)};\mathbb Z)\approx\mathbb Z_{k+1},\qquad
 H_2(Z^{(k)};\mathbb Z)\approx\mathbb Z^{m/2-2}\oplus\mathbb Z_{k+1},\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 H_3(Z^{(k)};\mathbb Z)=0.
\]
Moreover, their curvature energy, volume and diameter satisfy
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \int_{Z^{(k)}}|\operatorname{Rm}(g_Z^{(k)})|^2\,dV_{g_Z^{(k)}}=16\pi^2m,
 \\
 \operatorname{Vol}(Z^{(k)})=\frac{V_k}{k+1}=o(k^{-1}),
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \operatorname{diam}(Z^{(k)},g_Z^{(k)})\leqslant\pi.
 \end{gathered}
\]
In particular, the square quotients are rational homology four-spheres with the minimum curvature energy $64\pi^2$ for closed oriented positive Einstein four-manifolds, and the hexagon quotients have
the rational homology of $\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^2$ and curvature
energy $96\pi^2$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The free action above has order $k+1$, and $M^{(k)}$ is simply connected,
so $M^{(k)}\to Z^{(k)}$ is the universal cover and
$\pi_1(Z^{(k)})=\mathbb Z_{k+1}$.
The Einstein equation descends to the quotient. Multiplicativity of
Euler characteristic and signature gives
\[
 \chi(Z^{(k)})=\frac{\frac{m}2(k+1)}{k+1}=\frac{m}{2},\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \tau(Z^{(k)})=\frac{(k+1)(2-\frac{m}2)}{k+1}=2-\frac{m}{2}.
\]
Since $H_1(Z^{(k)};\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z_{k+1}$, Poincar\'e duality gives
$H_3(Z^{(k)};\mathbb Z)=H^1(Z^{(k)};\mathbb Z)=0$ and hence
$b_2(Z^{(k)})=\frac{m}{2}-2$. Poincar\'e duality and the universal coefficient
theorem identify the torsion subgroup of $H_2$ with
$\operatorname{Ext}(H_1,\mathbb Z)\approx\mathbb Z_{k+1}$, proving the
homology formulae.

As $g_Z^{(k)}$ is Einstein, \eqref{eq:CGB} and $\chi(Z^{(k)})=\frac{m}{2}$ give
\[
 \int_{Z^{(k)}}|\operatorname{Rm}(g_Z^{(k)})|^2\,dV_{g_Z^{(k)}}=32\pi^2\chi(Z^{(k)})=16\pi^2m.
\] The volume is divided by the covering
degree $k+1$, and $V_k\to0$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:volumes}. The diameter bound $\operatorname{diam}\leqslant\pi$ is the Bonnet-Myers theorem. Finally, any closed connected oriented positive
Einstein four-manifold $Y$ has $b_1(Y)=0$ by Bochner's formula, so \eqref{eq:CGB} gives
\[
 \int_Y|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\,dV=32\pi^2\chi(Y)
 =32\pi^2\bigl(2+b_2(Y)\bigr)\geqslant64\pi^2.
\]
Thus the square quotients attain the minimum. Orientability is needed since the round $\mathbb{RP}^4$ has energy $32\pi^2$.
