title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: compactness and limit of the  torus shape.}
By Lemma~ \ref{lem:smooth-cores}, the coefficients of $(h,\psi,\Phi)$ in the
normal chart at $o$ and in the cylinder are bounded in every $C^j$. A diagonal
subsequence therefore converges smoothly on every $E_\delta$.

The  lift of $\mathsf r$ acts on the torus angles by $\mathsf B$ of \eqref{eq:hexagon-symmetries} in the square case, where it exchanges the two circles, and by $\mathsf A$ in the hexagon case, by \eqref{eq:hexagon-lifts}. So the invariance of $g$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iota-equivariance}
 \Phi\circ\mathsf r=\iota\circ\Phi,\qquad\text{where}\qquad\iota(\Phi'):=\mathsf B\Phi'\mathsf B,\quad\text{respectively}\quad\iota(\Phi'):=\mathsf A^{-\mathsf T}\Phi'\mathsf A^{-1},
\end{equation}
and $\iota$ is an isometry of $\mathbb H^2$ fixing $\Phi_o$. In the square case, $\Phi_k$ lies on the diagonal geodesic, which $\iota$ reverses, with unique fixed point $\Phi_o$ on that geodesic. In the hexagon case, $\iota$ is a rotation of order three, with unique fixed point $\Phi_o$. The rotation $\mathsf r$  fixes $o$ and $\psi$, so it commutes with $\exp_o$ and with the flow of $V_\psi$, and it acts in both charts by $\Theta\mapsto\Theta+\frac{4\pi}{m(k+1)}$, which tends to the identity. Passing \eqref{eq:iota-equivariance} to the limit gives $\Phi_\infty=\iota\circ\Phi_\infty$, with $\Phi_\infty$ on the diagonal geodesic in the square case, so $\Phi_\infty\equiv\Phi_o$.

\emph{Step 2: identification of the limit.} Put $r:=\sqrt{\psi_\infty}$. Since $\Phi_\infty=\Phi_o$, \eqref{eq:concavity} and \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities} give
 \[
 \operatorname{Hess}_{h_\infty}r=-\frac{|dr|_{h_\infty}^2+3r^2}{2r}\,h_\infty,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad d\bigl(r|dr|_{h_\infty}^2+r^3\bigr)=0.
\]
 Since $r(o)=1$ and $dr(o)=0$, we get $|dr|_{h_\infty}^2=\frac{1}r-r^2=F(r)$. As the Hessian of $r$  is pure trace, $J\nabla r$ is a Killing field, where $J$ is the rotation by a right angle, and  $-\frac{2}{3}J\nabla r$ has period $2\pi$, since $\operatorname{Hess}_{h_\infty}r(o)=-\frac{3}{2}h_\infty(o)$. With the corresponding angle $\vartheta$, $h_\infty$ is \eqref{eq:kottler-orbit}, independently of the subsequence. 
 

\emph{Step 3: convergence of the orbit spaces.} By \eqref{eq:core-retraction}, the distance of $E_\delta$ is the restriction of the distance of $\overline\Omega^{(k)}$, so, by Step~2, the cores $E_\delta$ converge as metric spaces to $\{r^2\geqslant\delta\}\subset B_\infty$. By \eqref{eq:base-radius}, $E_\delta$ is $\arcsin\sqrt\delta$-dense in $\overline\Omega^{(k)}$, and $\{r^2\geqslant\delta\}$ has the same property in $B_\infty$ by \eqref{eq:kottler-orbit}, since $F(r)\geqslant1-r^2$.
Letting $k\to+\infty$ and then $\delta\to0$, the orbit spaces $(\overline\Omega^{(k)},d_h)$ converge to $B_\infty$. 

\emph{Step 4: collapse of the torus orbits.} The torus orbits collapse:  \eqref{eq:area-volume} for $g_{\beta_k}$, whose central torus is that of $g^{(k)}$ and whose volume is $\beta_kV_k$, Corollary~\ref{cor:volumes} and Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar}(c) give
 \[
 \rho_k(o)=\frac{\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)}{4\pi^2}\leqslant CV_k\longrightarrow0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \sup_{q\in\Omega^{(k)}}\operatorname{diam}\pi^{-1}(q)\leqslant2\operatorname{diam}(\Sigma)\leqslant C\sqrt{\rho_k(o)}\longrightarrow0,
\]
where the last bound uses that the central shape $\Phi_o$ is fixed. Since $\pi$ is a submetry onto $(\overline\Omega^{(k)},d_h)$, with fibers of diameter tending to zero, $(M^{(k)},g^{(k)})$ converges to $B_\infty$ in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense.

Finally, the metric \eqref{eq:kottler-orbit} has curvature $K_{h_\infty}=-\frac{1}{2}F''(r)=1-r^{-3}\leqslant0$, so,  with $\tau:=d_{h_\infty}(o,\cdot)$, the Rauch comparison theorem gives $h_\infty\geqslant d\tau^2+\tau^2d\vartheta^2$. Two boundary points with opposite angles $\vartheta$ are therefore at $h_\infty$-distance at least $\frac{2\pi}{3}$, the flat distance, and every point lies within $\frac{\pi}{3}$ of the center, so $\operatorname{diam}(B_\infty)=\frac{2\pi}{3}$. The dimension of $\partial B_\infty$ is computed in Remark~\ref{rem:four-thirds}.

label: rem:kottler
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:kottler}
The metric $h_\infty$ of \eqref{eq:kottler-orbit} is the orbit metric of $g_{\mathrm{Kot},\varepsilon}:=h_\infty+\varepsilon^2r^2(\Phi_o)_{ij}\,d\phi_i\,d\phi_j$, the Riemannian Kottler metric with flat toroidal horizon, cosmological constant $3$ and \textit{negative} mass $\mathfrak m=-\frac{1}{2}$, so that $F=-2\mathfrak m/r-r^2$ \cite{Kot18}, which satisfies $\operatorname{Ric}(g_{\mathrm{Kot},\varepsilon})=3g_{\mathrm{Kot},\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. The parameter $\varepsilon$ is the size of the flat torus orbits. Its end $r\to0$ is asymptotic to a Kasner metric with exponents $(-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})$, with the exponent $-\frac{1}{3}$ belonging to the $\vartheta$-circle.
head: environment

label: rem:four-thirds
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:four-thirds}
Let $t:=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\arccos r^{3/2}$ be the distance to $\partial B_\infty$. Then we have $r^{3/2}=\sin\frac{3t}{2}$, so $\frac{4}{9}F(r)=\frac{4}{9}\cos^2\bigl(\frac{3t}{2}\bigr)\sin^{-2/3}\bigl(\frac{3t}{2}\bigr)$, and, with the $2\pi$-periodic coordinate $\vartheta$ of \eqref{eq:kottler-orbit}, the metric reads
\[
 h_\infty=dt^2+\Bigl(\frac{2}{3}\Bigr)^{8/3}t^{-2/3}\bigl(1+O(t^2)\bigr)\,d\vartheta^2\qquad \text{ as }t\to 0.
\]
This is a Grushin-type metric: in the notation $dr^2+r^{-4\alpha}dv^2$ of \cite[Section~3.1]{DHPW23}, $\alpha=\frac{1}{6}$. By \cite[Theorem~3.5]{DHPW23}, $\partial B_\infty$ is of Hausdorff dimension $\frac{4}{3}$, while $B_\infty$ itself has dimension $2$. Collapsed Ricci limits of non-integer dimension also appear in \cite{PW22,Pan23}.

label: rem:segment-limit
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:segment-limit}
The generator  $\varpi_k$ of Section~\ref{sec:proof-main} acts on $\Omega^{(k)}$ by $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$, that is, by $\vartheta\mapsto\vartheta+\frac{2\pi}{k+1}$ in the normal angle of the limit in Theorem~\ref{thm:collapsed-limit}. Since the rotations of $\vartheta$ are isometries of $h_\infty$, equivariant Gromov-Hausdorff convergence shows that the quotients $(Z^{(k)},g_Z^{(k)})$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-fundamental-groups} converge to $B_\infty/{\mathbb S^1}=[0,\frac{\pi}{3}]$, parametrized by the distance to the center. By Lemma~ \ref{lem:smooth-cores}, $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_Z^{(k)})|$ stays bounded over each core, while $\max|\operatorname{Rm}(g_Z^{(k)})|\to+\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:curvature-localization}(i), so the curvature diverges only at the end $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

label: thm:periodic-models
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:periodic-models}


Put $\Lambda_k:=\max|\operatorname{Rm}(g_Z^{(k)})|$, and let $c_k$ be the corner of $Z^{(k)}$ at the end of a rod with rod vector $\pm e_1$, for the boundary orientation of $\Omega_Z^{(k)}$. Then $\Lambda_k\to+\infty$, and the whole sequence satisfies
\[
 (Z^{(k)},\Lambda_kg_Z^{(k)},c_k)\longrightarrow(X,g_X,c)
\]
smoothly on compact subsets. The limit $(X,g_X)$ has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item \emph{Curvature.} It is complete, nonflat and Ricci-flat, with $|\operatorname{Rm}|\leqslant1$ and $\int_X|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\,dV=32\pi^2\chi(X)=16\pi^2m$, the curvature energy of every $Z^{(k)}$.
\item \emph{Torus action.} It has an effective isometric action of $\mathbb R^2/2\pi\mathbb Z^2$ generated by the limits of $X_1,X_2$.  Its orbit space is  a closed half-cylinder, whose boundary circle  consists of $\frac{m}{2}$ rods, with rod vectors $(e_1,e_2)$ in the square case and $(e_1,e_1+e_2,e_2)$ in the hexagon case, in cyclic order, permuted cyclically by an isometry of $X$.
\item \emph{Kasner end.}  Its end is asymptotic to  a Kasner metric with exponents $(-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})$.
\end{enumerate}
We write $X_{\mathrm{sq}}$ and $X_{\mathrm{hex}}$ for $X$, and $g_{\mathrm{sq}}$ and $g_{\mathrm{hex}}$ for $g_X$, in the two cases.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $X_{\mathrm{sq}}\approx {\mathbb S^4}\setminus {\mathbb T^2}$, and $g_{\mathrm{sq}}$ is a
one-period quotient of an equal-rod Euclidean
Myers-Korotkin-Nicolai metric \cite{My87,KN94,KRWY22}.
\item $X_{\mathrm{hex}}\approx\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^2\setminus {\mathbb T^2}$,
$\pi_1(X_{\mathrm{hex}})=\mathbb Z$, and $X_{\mathrm{hex}}$ contains compact fixed spheres of self-intersection $-1$. In particular, it is not spin.
The metric $g_{\mathrm{hex}}$ is not locally Hermitian in either orientation, and it is not static for any choice of generators of the torus action.
\end{enumerate}
In both cases the removed torus is a principal orbit of the standard
torus action.

label: lem:curvature-localization
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Since $\int_{Z^{(k)}}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2=16\pi^2m$ and $\operatorname{Vol}(Z^{(k)})=V_k/(k+1)\to0$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:volumes}, we have $\Lambda_k^2\geqslant16\pi^2m/\operatorname{Vol}(Z^{(k)})\to+\infty$.

(ii) Put $g_k':=Q_kg_{Z,k}$. The small-energy curvature estimate \cite[Theorem~0.8, p.~489]{CT06}, which assumes no lower volume bound, gives $\varepsilon_0,C_0>0$ such that every Einstein metric with $\operatorname{Ric}=\lambda g$, $|\lambda|\leqslant3$ and $\int_{B(p,1)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\leqslant\varepsilon_0$ satisfies $|\operatorname{Rm}|(p)\leqslant C_0$. Fix $A>\max\{1,\sqrt{C_0}\}$. For large $k$, the metric $A^{-2}g_k'$ has Einstein constant $3A^2Q_k^{-1}\leqslant3$ and curvature $A^2>C_0$ at $y_k$, while $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_k')|\leqslant4$ on $B_{g_k'}(y_k,A)$, since $Q_kr_k^2\to+\infty$. The scale invariance of the energy and the Bishop-Gromov inequality for $\operatorname{Ric}(g_k')\geqslant0$ therefore give
\[
 \varepsilon_0<\int_{B_{g_k'}(y_k,A)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\,dV\leqslant16\operatorname{Vol}_{g_k'}B(y_k,A)\leqslant16A^4\operatorname{Vol}_{g_k'}B(y_k,1).
\]
So Einstein regularity with \cite{And89} gives smooth subconvergence of $(Z^{(k)},g_k',y_k)$ to a complete Ricci-flat limit, with curvature energy at most $16\pi^2m$ by scale invariance, nonflat since $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_k')|(y_k)=1$. The points of $Z^{(k)}$ fixed by the torus are its corners (Section~\ref{subsec:free-quotients}), so Lemma~\ref{lem:torus-limit}(b), applied with $U_k:=Z^{(k)}$, gives corners $c_k$ with $\sup_kd_{g_k'}(y_k,c_k)<+\infty$. Since $\psi_k(c_k)=0$ and $\psi_k$ is $2$-Lipschitz for $g_{Z,k}$, by \eqref{eq:base-radius}, which passes to $\Omega_Z^{(k)}$, we have, for $0<\delta<1$,
\[
 d_{g_k'}\bigl(y_k,\{\psi_k\geqslant\delta\}\bigr)\geqslant\tfrac\delta2Q_k^{1/2}-d_{g_k'}(y_k,c_k)\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
So $\Sigma_Z$, the only orbit of $Z^{(k)}$ other than principal orbits, rods and corners, escapes, and Lemma~\ref{lem:torus-limit}(a), with the corners $c_k$, gives the limiting action. Its convergence maps preserve the stabilizers, so it has no orbit with nontrivial finite stabilizer.

(iii)  Otherwise, there are $x_k\in Z^{(k)}$ with $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_{Z,k})|(x_k)\varrho_k^2\to+\infty$, where $\varrho_k:=\frac{1}{2}d_{g_{Z,k}}(x_k,\mathcal C_k)\leqslant\frac{\pi}{2}$, by Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-fundamental-groups}. Let $y_k$ maximize $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_{Z,k})|(y)\bigl(\varrho_k-d_{g_{Z,k}}(x_k,y)\bigr)^2$ over $\overline B_{g_{Z,k}}(x_k,\varrho_k)$, and put
 \[
 r_k:=\tfrac12\bigl(\varrho_k-d_{g_{Z,k}}(x_k,y_k)\bigr)\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_k:=|\operatorname{Rm}(g_{Z,k})|(y_k).
\]
Then $Q_kr_k^2\to+\infty$, hence $Q_k\to+\infty$, and $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_{Z,k})|\leqslant4Q_k$ on $B_{g_{Z,k}}(y_k,r_k)$, while $d_{g_{Z,k}}(y_k,\mathcal C_k)\geqslant\varrho_k\geqslant2r_k$. So (ii) gives corners at  $g_{Z,k}$-distance at most $CQ_k^{-1/2}=o(r_k)$ from $y_k$,  a contradiction, which proves \eqref{eq:curvature-away-corners}.

label: lem:corner-noncollapse
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We choose the level set $\sigma_k$ of $\rho_k$ whose length $L_k$ equals the minimum of $|d\ell_k|_{h_k}^{-1}$ on $\sigma_k$, see \eqref{eq:rho-level-choice}. The annulus $\{t_k\leqslant\rho_k\leqslant2t_k\}$ then has width and circumference comparable to $L_k$, by \eqref{eq:rho-annulus-metric}, hence base area at least $C^{-1}L_k^2$, and Step~3 shows that its torus orbits have area at least $C^{-1}L_k^2$. We use the reduced data $h_k,\rho_k,\Phi_k$ of $g_{Z,k}$, with $\ell_k:=\log\rho_k$ and  $\psi_k=\rho_k/\rho_k(o)$, on the orbit space $\Omega_Z^{(k)}$ of Section~\ref{subsec:free-quotients}, the quotient of $\Omega^{(k)}$ by the rotation induced by  $\varpi_k$, of order $k+1$. The estimates \eqref{eq:base-radius} and \eqref{eq:core-coordinates}, the flow of $V_\psi$ and the retractions  of Lemma~\ref{lem:core-retraction}  pass to $\Omega_Z^{(k)}$. Below, $C$ denotes constants independent of $k$.

\emph{Step 1: the level set $\sigma_k$.}  Away from $o$, put $\varkappa:=|d\ell_k|_{h_k}^{-1}$, and let $N:=\varkappa\nabla_{h_k}\ell_k$ be the ascending unit normal to the level sets of $\rho_k$.  The Hessian identity in \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities}, $K_{h_k}\leqslant1$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:bochner}) and $B\geqslant0$ give
\[
 N\varkappa=-\varkappa^2\operatorname{Hess}_{h_k}\ell_k(N,N)\geqslant\tfrac12+2\varkappa^2.
\]
So the minimum of $\varkappa$ on the level sets of $\rho_k$ strictly increases along the flow of $V_\psi$, whereas their lengths strictly decrease, by \eqref{eq:core-coordinates}. As $\varkappa=\psi_k/|d\psi_k|_{h_k}$, \eqref{eq:base-radius} gives
\[
 \frac{\psi_k}{2\sqrt{1-\psi_k^2}}\leqslant\varkappa\leqslant\frac12\sqrt{\frac{\psi_k}{1-\psi_k}}.
\]
Hence near $\partial\Omega_Z^{(k)}$, $\varkappa\to0$ while, for fixed $k$, the lengths stay bounded below, and near $o$, $\varkappa\to+\infty$ while the lengths tend to zero. So there is a unique level set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-level-choice}
 \sigma_k:=\{\rho_k=t_k\}\qquad\text{with}\qquad L_k:=\operatorname{Length}_{h_k}(\sigma_k)=\min_{\sigma_k}\varkappa.
\end{equation}
 Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-cores}, the level set $\{\psi_k=\delta\}$ of $\Omega^{(k)}$ has length at most $C_\delta$, so its image in $\Omega_Z^{(k)}$ has length at most $C_\delta/(k+1)$, which is smaller than $\frac{\delta}{2}\leqslant\min\varkappa$ there for large $k$. Hence $t_k<\delta\rho_k(o)$ for large $k$, so $t_k/\rho_k(o)\to0$ and $L_k\to0$.


On $\{\rho_k\leqslant2t_k\}$,  for large $k$,  the same identity and $\Delta_{h_k}\ell_k=-6-\varkappa^{-2}$ give $-Ch_k\leqslant\varkappa^2\operatorname{Hess}_{h_k}\ell_k\leqslant-\frac{1}{2}N^\flat\otimes N^\flat$. As $d\varkappa=-\varkappa^2\operatorname{Hess}_{h_k}\ell_k(N,\cdot)$, this gives, for $J$ tangent to the level sets of $\rho_k$,
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-level-derivatives}
 \tfrac12\leqslant N\varkappa,\qquad |d\varkappa|_{h_k}\leqslant C,\qquad\text{and}\qquad -C|J|_{h_k}^2\leqslant\varkappa^2\operatorname{Hess}_{h_k}\ell_k(J,J)\leqslant0.
\end{equation}
 Integrating $|d\varkappa|_{h_k}\leqslant C$ along $\sigma_k$,  of length $L_k=\min_{\sigma_k}\varkappa$, gives $L_k\leqslant\varkappa\leqslant CL_k$ on $\sigma_k$.

Let $\theta\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the arclength of $\sigma_k$ divided by $L_k$, transported along the flow of $V_\psi$, and put $u:=\log(\rho_k/t_k)$. Then  $h_k=\varkappa^2du^2+|\partial_\theta|_{h_k}^2d\theta^2$, $\partial_u\log\varkappa=N\varkappa$ and, by \eqref{eq:core-coordinates}, $\frac{1}{2}\partial_u|\partial_\theta|_{h_k}^2=\varkappa^2\operatorname{Hess}_{h_k}\ell_k(\partial_\theta,\partial_\theta)$. On $\{0\leqslant u\leqslant\log2\}$, \eqref{eq:rho-level-derivatives}  therefore gives $C^{-1}L_k\leqslant\varkappa\leqslant CL_k$ and $C^{-1}L_k\leqslant|\partial_\theta|_{h_k}\leqslant L_k$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-annulus-metric}
 C^{-1}L_k^2(du^2+d\theta^2)\leqslant h_k\leqslant CL_k^2(du^2+d\theta^2)\qquad\text{on }\{t_k\leqslant\rho_k\leqslant2t_k\}.
\end{equation}
For $u\leqslant0$,  $\partial_u\log\varkappa\geqslant\frac{1}{2}$ gives $\varkappa(u,\theta)\leqslant e^{u/2}\varkappa(0,\theta)$, so each descending curve $\{\theta=\theta_0,\ u\leqslant0\}$ has length at most  $2\varkappa(0,\theta_0)\leqslant CL_k$. Let $P_k$ be the retraction of Lemma~\ref{lem:core-retraction} onto $\{\rho_k\geqslant t_k\}$, which maps each such curve to its initial point. Then $d_{h_k}(y,P_k(y))\leqslant CL_k$ for $y\in\{\rho_k<t_k\}$, and, by continuity, for $y\in\mathcal C_k$. A corner $c$ is fixed by the torus, so $d_{g_{Z,k}}(c,x)=d_{h_k}(c,\pi(x))$ for $x\in Z^{(k)}$, and, as $\sigma_k$ has length $L_k$, this gives the first inequality of \eqref{eq:corner-noncollapse}.

\emph{Step 2: a short path to a regular rod.} We find a short path from $\sigma_k$ to an open rod which avoids the corners, so that the curvature is controlled along it. There are at most $\frac{m}{2}$ points $P_k(c)$, $c\in\mathcal C_k$, on $\sigma_k$, which has $\theta$-length one, so the midpoint $x_k$ of a largest arc of $\sigma_k$ between them has $\theta$-distance at least $\frac{1}m$ from all of them. By \eqref{eq:rho-annulus-metric}, a path in $\{\rho_k\geqslant t_k\}$ from $x_k$ to $P_k(c)$ has length at least $C^{-1}L_k$: if it stays in $\{\rho_k\leqslant2t_k\}$, its $\theta$-length is at least $\frac{1}m$, and otherwise its $u$-length is at least $\log2$. By \eqref{eq:core-retraction}, $d_{h_k}(x_k,P_k(c))\geqslant C^{-1}L_k$. Let $\gamma_k$ be the descending curve from $x_k$. Since $P_k$ is $1$-Lipschitz and constant on $\gamma_k$, every $y\in\gamma_k$ satisfies $d_{h_k}(y,c)\geqslant C^{-1}L_k$ for $c\in\mathcal C_k$. So $\gamma_k$ has length at most $CL_k$ and ends at a point $e_k$ of an open rod. Hence the horizontal lift  $\widetilde\gamma_k$ of $\gamma_k$, from  $\widetilde x_k$ over $x_k$ to  $\widetilde e_k$ over $e_k$, stays at $g_{Z,k}$-distance at least $C^{-1}L_k$ from $\mathcal C_k$, and \eqref{eq:curvature-away-corners} gives $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_{Z,k})|\leqslant CL_k^{-2}$ along  $\widetilde\gamma_k$.

\emph{ Step 3: the torus scale.} The Killing field of the rod vector at the end of this path vanishes there, and its derivative is the rotation by a right angle of the normal plane, by the smooth angle condition; transporting its value and derivative to $\sigma_k$ along the path bounds the orbit area from below. On $\sigma_k$,  $|d\Phi_k|_{h_k}^2=4K_{h_k}+|d\ell_k|_{h_k}^2\leqslant4+\varkappa^{-2}$, so $\int_{\sigma_k}|d\Phi_k|_{h_k}\,ds_{h_k}\leqslant C$. The isometry $\mathsf s_k$ of Section~\ref{subsec:models} preserves  $\sigma_k$, and an arc of $\sigma_k$ joins  each $y\in\sigma_k$ to $\mathsf s_k(y)$, so \eqref{eq:iota-equivariance} and \eqref{eq:cyclic-displacement}  give  $d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi_k(y),\Phi_o)\leqslant C$, that is, $\Phi_k\leqslant C\Phi_o$ on $\sigma_k$. Let $v$ be the rod vector at $e_k$, and $X_v:=v_1X_1+v_2X_2$. By \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-side},  $X_v(\widetilde e_k)=0$ and $|\nabla X_v|(\widetilde e_k)=\sqrt2$. The block form \eqref{eq:matrix-ansatz} gives  $|\nabla X_v|\leqslant C(|d\ell_k|_{h_k}+|d\Phi_k|_{h_k})|X_v|$ on principal orbits, and  at $\widetilde x_k$ we have $|d\ell_k|_{h_k}+|d\Phi_k|_{h_k}\leqslant CL_k^{-1}$ and $|X_v|^2=t_k\Phi_k(v,v)\leqslant Ct_k$. So \eqref{eq:killing-transport} along  $\widetilde\gamma_k$, with $r:=L_k$, gives
\[
 \sqrt2=|\nabla X_v|(\widetilde e_k)\leqslant C\bigl(L_k^{-1}|X_v|+|\nabla X_v|\bigr)(\widetilde x_k)\leqslant C\,\frac{\sqrt{t_k}}{L_k},\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad t_k\geqslant C^{-1}L_k^2.
\]

\emph{Step  4:  the volume.}  By Step~1 and \eqref{eq:rho-annulus-metric}, the corners and the points of $\{t_k\leqslant\rho_k\leqslant2t_k\}$ lie within $h_k$-distance $CL_k$ of $\sigma_k$,  so the preimage of this annulus lies in $B_{g_{Z,k}}(c,CL_k)$  for every $c\in\mathcal C_k$. Its base has $h_k$-area  at least $C^{-1}L_k^2$, by \eqref{eq:rho-annulus-metric}, and its torus orbits have area $4\pi^2\rho_k\geqslant4\pi^2t_k\geqslant C^{-1}L_k^2$, by \eqref{eq:scalar-volume} and Step~3. This gives the second inequality of \eqref{eq:corner-noncollapse}.

label: prop:corner-compactness
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:curvature-localization}, $\Lambda_k\to+\infty$ and \eqref{eq:curvature-away-corners} holds. Let $p_k$ satisfy $|\operatorname{Rm}(g_{Z,k})|(p_k)=\Lambda_k$. Lemma~\ref{lem:curvature-localization}(ii), with $y_k:=p_k$ and $r_k:=\pi$, gives a subsequence of $(Z^{(k)},\Lambda_kg_{Z,k},p_k)$ converging to a complete, nonflat and Ricci-flat limit $(X,g_X,p)$ with a torus action as in the statement, and corners $c_k$ with $\Lambda_k^{1/2}d_{g_{Z,k}}(p_k,c_k)\leqslant C$.

 Along a minimizing geodesic between two distinct corners, some combination of $X_1,X_2$ restricts to a nonzero Jacobi field vanishing at both ends, since, by the corner model \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-corner}, the derivatives at a corner of the Killing fields of the two adjacent rod vectors are the rotations of two orthogonal planes, so they do not both vanish on a nonzero tangent vector. As $\sec(\Lambda_kg_{Z,k})\leqslant1$, this geodesic has $\Lambda_kg_{Z,k}$ -length at least $\pi$, which is the first inequality of \eqref{eq:corner-distances}, compare \cite[proof of Lemma~9]{Don08}.

Suppose that $\Lambda_kL_k^2\to+\infty$ along a subsequence. By Lemma~\ref{lem:corner-noncollapse} and the Bishop-Gromov inequality for $\operatorname{Ric}(g_{Z,k})=3g_{Z,k}$, $\operatorname{Vol}_{g_{Z,k}}B_{g_{Z,k}}(c_k,r)\geqslant C^{-1}r^4$ for $0<r\leqslant CL_k$, that is, $\operatorname{Vol}_{\Lambda_kg_{Z,k}}B(c_k,s)\geqslant C^{-1}s^4$ for $0<s\leqslant C\Lambda_k^{1/2}L_k$. As $c_k$ stays at bounded $\Lambda_kg_{Z,k}$-distance from $p_k$, the limit $X$ has Euclidean volume growth, and its curvature energy is at most $16\pi^2m$, since $\int|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\,dV$ is invariant under rescaling. By Corollary~\ref{cor:ale-exclusion}, whose determinant hypothesis holds by \eqref{eq:rod-determinant}, it is flat, a contradiction. Hence $\Lambda_kL_k^2\leqslant C$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:corner-noncollapse} gives the second inequality of \eqref{eq:corner-distances}. For distinct corners $c,c'$, \eqref{eq:corner-distances} and \eqref{eq:corner-noncollapse} give $\pi\leqslant\Lambda_k^{1/2}d_{g_{Z,k}}(c,c')\leqslant C\Lambda_k^{1/2}L_k$, which is the lower bound in \eqref{eq:scale-comparison}.

So all corners lie at bounded $\Lambda_kg_{Z,k}$-distance from $p_k$, and the limit may be based at $c:=\lim c_k$: $(Z^{(k)},\Lambda_kg_{Z,k},c_k)\to(X,g_X,c)$, with $|\operatorname{Rm}|\leqslant1$ and $\int_X|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\leqslant16\pi^2m$. The convergence maps of Lemma~\ref{lem:torus-limit}(a) preserve the stabilizers, so the corners of $X$ are the limits of corners of $Z^{(k)}$, and, by \eqref{eq:corner-distances}, all $\frac{m}{2}$ corners converge, with distinct limits.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Local equations.} By the scaling rules at the beginning of Section~\ref{subsec:models}, the Einstein constant of $\Lambda_kg_{Z,k}$ is $3\Lambda_k^{-1}\to0$, so \eqref{eq:Einstein-identities}, Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar}(a) and \eqref{eq:concavity} give,  in the limit, $\Delta_h\rho=0$, $K_h\leqslant0$ and $\operatorname{Hess}_h\sqrt\rho\leqslant0$ on the principal part of $X$. If $\rho$ had an interior critical point $x_*$, then $\operatorname{Hess}_h\sqrt\rho\leqslant0$, restricted to the geodesics from $x_*$, would make $x_*$ a local maximum of $\rho$, and the strong maximum principle for the harmonic function $\rho$ would force $\rho$ to be constant, which contradicts $\rho=0$ at a corner. So $dz:=*d\rho$ gives local Weyl coordinates, in which \eqref{eq:weyl-harmonic} and \eqref{eq:weyl-nu} are the standard Weyl equations \cite[Section~2]{LS25}. The bound $K_h\leqslant0$ reads $|D\Phi|\leqslant\rho^{-1}$, since $4K_h=|d\Phi|_h^2-|d\ell|_h^2$. Then \eqref{eq:weyl-nu} gives the bounds on $\partial_\rho a_{\mathrm W}$ in \eqref{eq:weyl-bounds}.

\emph{Orbit space.} Put $V_\rho:=\nabla_h\rho/|d\rho|_h^2$, so that $|V_\rho|_h=e^{a_{\mathrm W}}$ in local Weyl coordinates. By \eqref{eq:weyl-bounds}, along a flow line of $V_\rho$ parametrized by $\rho$,  the speed $|V_\rho|_h$ is nonincreasing  and at most $(\rho_1/\rho)^{1/2}|V_\rho|_h(\rho_1)$ for $\rho<\rho_1$. By completeness, every flow line is defined for all $\rho\in(0,+\infty)$ and has finite length as $\rho\downarrow0$. Its endpoint is a rod or corner point, by Proposition~\ref{prop:corner-compactness}. The flow identifies the interior $\Omega_X$ of $\overline\Omega_X$ with $(0,+\infty)\times\{\rho=1\}$, so the level set $\{\rho=1\}$ is connected, hence a line or a circle.

The isometry $\mathsf s_k$ of Section~\ref{subsec:models}, which satisfies $\Phi_k\circ\mathsf s_k=\iota\circ\Phi_k$ by \eqref{eq:iota-equivariance},  moves a corner by a bounded $\Lambda_kh_k$-distance, by \eqref{eq:corner-distances}. The Arzel\`a-Ascoli theorem, applied to $\mathsf s_k$ and $\mathsf s_k^{-1}$ on the converging orbit spaces, gives a subsequence converging, smoothly on the interior, to an orientation-preserving isometry $\mathsf s$ of $h$ with $\rho\circ\mathsf s=\rho$ and $\Phi\circ\mathsf s=\iota\circ\Phi$. As the corners of $X$ are the distinct limits of those of $Z^{(k)}$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:corner-compactness}, $\mathsf s$ maps each corner to an adjacent one, and has order $\frac{m}{2}\geqslant2$. Since $\mathsf s$ preserves $\rho$, it commutes with the flow of $V_\rho$, so it restricts to an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $\{\rho=1\}$ of order $\frac{m}{2}$, which is impossible on a line. Hence $\{\rho=1\}$ is a circle, and the closed form $dz=*d\rho$ integrates to a coordinate $z\in\mathbb R/P_{\mathrm W}\mathbb Z$ on $\Omega_X$, with $P_{\mathrm W}:=\int_{\{\rho=1\}}*d\rho$.

\emph{Boundary.} Let $w=x+iy$ be a conformal chart of a rod or corner model \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-side}, respectively \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-corner}, of $g_X$. The odd extension of $\rho$ is harmonic, so $\rho+iz$ is, up to a constant, a holomorphic function of $w$. At a rod point $(0,y_0)$, where $\rho=xe^{\bar\ell}$, its derivative is $e^{\bar\ell(0,y_0)}\neq0$. At a corner, where $\rho=xye^{\widehat\ell}$, the oddness of $\rho$ in $x$ and in $y$ excludes a linear term, and its leading term is $-\frac{i}{2}e^{\widehat\ell(0)}w^2$, which maps the quadrant onto a half-plane. We may therefore replace the corner chart by the first-quadrant branch of $x+iy:=\sqrt{2i(\rho+i(z-z_*))}$, where $z_*$ is the $z$-coordinate of the corner and the two adjacent rods are suitably ordered: by the double-zero expansion, this is a smooth change of conformal coordinates with nonzero derivative, preserving the parities, and $\rho=xy$, $z-z_*=\frac{1}{2}(y^2-x^2)$, compare \cite[Section~6]{CS04}. In both cases, $(\rho,z)$ extends to a homeomorphism from a neighborhood of the point in $\overline\Omega_X$ onto a relative neighborhood of a point of $\{\rho=0\}$. With the flow of $V_\rho$, $\overline\Omega_X$ is therefore homeomorphic to the closed half-cylinder $[0,+\infty)\times\mathbb R/P_{\mathrm W}\mathbb Z$.

As $\mathsf s$ preserves $\rho$ and $dz$, it is a translation in $z$. Since it maps each of the $\frac{m}{2}$ corners to an adjacent one, changing the sign of $z$ if necessary, it is  $z\mapsto z+\frac{2P_{\mathrm W}}m$, so the rod endpoints are equally spaced in $z$, and $\Phi\circ\mathsf s=\iota\circ\Phi$ is \eqref{eq:weyl-shift}.

\emph{Angular period.} Since the distribution orthogonal to the orbits is integrable, by \eqref{eq:matrix-ansatz}, a horizontal lift of a circuit of the $z$-circle closes up to a torus translation independent of the circuit; we show that this translation vanishes. The surfaces $\{\boldsymbol\phi=\mathrm{const}\}$ of $M^{(k)}$ are orthogonal to the torus orbits, by \eqref{eq:matrix-ansatz}. Lift a loop going once around the image of $o$ in $\Omega_Z^{(k)}$, in the direction of increasing $\theta$, orthogonally to the orbits. Starting at $(\theta_0,\boldsymbol\phi_0)$ in $M^{(k)}$, the lift ends at
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:quotient-angular-displacement}
 (\theta_0+\pi,\boldsymbol\phi_0)=\varpi_k\Bigl(\theta_0,\boldsymbol\phi_0-\frac{2\pi}{k+1}\,e_1\Bigr).
\end{equation}
So, in $Z^{(k)}$, the lift ends on its initial orbit, with angular displacement $-\frac{2\pi}{k+1}e_1$. Closing it in this orbit gives a loop whose lift to $M^{(k)}$ joins $p:=(\theta_0,\boldsymbol\phi_0)$ to  $\varpi_kp$, hence generates $\pi_1(Z^{(k)})=\mathbb Z_{k+1}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-fundamental-groups}).   A loop going once around the orbit cylinder is the limit of loops going once around the image of $o$ in the quotient orbit spaces $\Omega_Z^{(k)}$: equivariant convergence identifies the neighborhoods of all rods and corners, in their cyclic order. By Proposition~\ref{prop:corner-compactness}, the metrics and the original torus generators converge, without change of integral basis, so the angular displacement $-\frac{2\pi}{k+1}e_1$ of these loops, given by \eqref{eq:quotient-angular-displacement}, tends to zero in the fixed torus. Thus the angular identification is $(z,\boldsymbol\phi)\sim(z+P_{\mathrm W},\boldsymbol\phi)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:corner-compactness} and Lemma~\ref{lem:weyl}, it remains to prove the Kasner asymptotics, the  uniqueness of the limit,  which gives the convergence of the whole sequence, the topology, the curvature energy and the identifications.


\emph{Kasner asymptotics.}
By \eqref{eq:weyl-shift} and \eqref{eq:cyclic-displacement}, with $\Phi$ on the diagonal geodesic in the square case by \eqref{eq:ansatz}, and by the bound $|D\Phi|\leqslant\rho^{-1}$ of \eqref{eq:weyl-bounds}, we have
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:end-shape}
 d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi(\rho,z),\Phi_o)
 \leqslant
 d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi(\rho,z),\Phi(\rho,z+\tfrac{2P_{\mathrm W}}m))
 \leqslant\frac{2P_{\mathrm W}}{m\rho}.
\end{equation}
Let $\Delta_3:=\partial_\rho^2+\rho^{-1}\partial_\rho+\partial_z^2$ be the Euclidean Laplacian on axisymmetric functions. By Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-calculus}(iii), \eqref{eq:weyl-harmonic} reads $\Delta_3\Phi=|D\Phi|^2\Phi$, so $U:=\Pi_{\Phi_o}\Phi$ of \eqref{eq:central-matrix-coordinate} satisfies
\[
 \Delta_3U=|D\Phi|^2U.
\]
By \eqref{eq:end-shape} and $|U|_o=\sinh d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi_o)$, we have $U=O(\rho^{-1})$, and $|D\Phi|\leqslant\rho^{-1}$, so $\Delta_3U=O(\rho^{-3})$.
Rescaled interior estimates \cite[Theorems~9.11 and~6.2]{GT01} on balls of radius $\rho/4$ in the
periodic lift, followed by differentiation of the equation $\Delta_3U=|D\Phi|^2U$, give
\[
 |D^jU|\leqslant C_j\rho^{-1-j},
 \qquad\text{for }j\geqslant0.
\]

\emph{The conformal factor.} The quadratures \eqref{eq:weyl-nu} then give
$D(a_{\mathrm W}+\frac{1}{4}\log\rho)=O(\rho^{-3})$.
Integration in $\rho$, and the $z$-equation, give a constant $c_{\mathrm K}$
such that
\[
 \left|D^j\left(a_{\mathrm W}+\tfrac14\log\rho-c_{\mathrm K}\right)\right|
 \leqslant C_j\rho^{-2-j},\qquad\text{for }j\geqslant0.
\]
By \eqref{eq:weyl}, these are the asserted asymptotics to
$e^{2c_{\mathrm K}}\rho^{-1/2}(d\rho^2+dz^2)
+\rho(\Phi_o)_{ij}\,d\phi_i\,d\phi_j$.
With $\varsigma:=\frac{4}{3}e^{c_{\mathrm K}}\rho^{3/4}$, this model has Kasner
exponents $(-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})$.

\emph{Uniqueness of the limit.} Let $(X',g_{X'},c')$ be the limit along another subsequence, with Weyl coordinates $(\rho',z')$, shape $\Phi'$ and conformal factor $a_{\mathrm W}'$. The homothety $g_{X'}\mapsto\lambda g_{X'}$, with $\lambda:=P_{\mathrm W}/P_{\mathrm W}'$, multiplies $\rho'$ and $z'$ by $\lambda$, so we may assume that both Weyl periods equal $P_{\mathrm W}$. Normalize $z$ and $z'$ to vanish at $c$ and $c'$. By the choice of the corners $c_k$, the two orbit spaces then have the same rod endpoints  $\frac{2P_{\mathrm W}}m\mathbb Z$ and the same rod vectors, in the same cyclic order, and both have the untwisted angular identification of Lemma~\ref{lem:weyl}.

Identify  the two orbit spaces through $(\rho',z')=(\rho,z)$. At a corner, work in the common integral basis of the two adjacent rod vectors, ordered so that they collapse on $\{x=0\}$ and  $\{y=0\}$, respectively, and in the coordinates $\rho=xy$, $z-z_*=\frac{1}{2}(y^2-x^2)$ of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:weyl},  which are the same for both metrics. With $C:=\rho^{-1/2}\operatorname{diag}(x,y)$, \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-corner} gives
\[
 \Phi=C\widehat GC^{\mathsf T},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \Phi'=C\widehat G'C^{\mathsf T},
\]
 where $\widehat G$ and $\widehat G'$  have determinant one, as $\rho=xy$. The map $S\mapsto CSC^{\mathsf T}$ is an isometry of $\mathbb H^2$, so $d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi')=d_{\mathbb H^2}(\widehat G,\widehat G')$, which is bounded near the corner since $\widehat G$ and $\widehat G'$ are smooth and positive definite.  Near a rod point,  the same argument applies  in a common rod-adapted integral basis, with the common conformal coordinate $\rho+iz$ and $C:=\rho^{-1/2}\operatorname{diag}(\rho,1)$. These unimodular changes of basis act in the same way on both metrics and preserve their hyperbolic distance. Put $u:=d_{\mathbb H^2}(\Phi,\Phi')^2$. By \eqref{eq:weyl-harmonic}, $\Phi$ and $\Phi'$ are harmonic maps to $\mathbb H^2$ for the flat metric $d\rho^2+\rho^2d\vartheta^2+dz^2$, whose Laplacian on functions of $(\rho,z)$ is $\Delta_3$, so the convexity of the squared distance on $\mathbb H^2\times\mathbb H^2$ gives $\Delta_3u\geqslant0$. As $u$ is bounded near the axis, which has codimension two in $D_R^2\times(\mathbb R/P_{\mathrm W}\mathbb Z)$, the maximum principle  of \cite[Section~2]{Wei95} gives $\sup_{\{\rho<R\}}u\leqslant\sup_{\{\rho=R\}}u$, and the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $R\to+\infty$, by \eqref{eq:end-shape}. Hence $\Phi'=\Phi$.

The quadratures \eqref{eq:weyl-nu} then show that $a_{\mathrm W}'-a_{\mathrm W}$ is constant, and the angle condition of \eqref{eq:matrix-smooth-side} on any rod makes it vanish. Hence the rescaled $g_{X'}$ is isometric to $g_X$, by an isometry which maps $c'$ to $c$ and preserves the torus generators.  The original subsequential limits both satisfy $\max|\operatorname{Rm}|=1$, since the points of maximal curvature of Proposition~\ref{prop:corner-compactness} stay at bounded distance from the corners,  so the isometry between $g_X$ and $\lambda g_{X'}$ forces $\lambda=1$. All subsequential limits therefore coincide, and the whole sequence converges.


\emph{Topology.} Fill the principal boundary of $\{\rho\leqslant\rho_0\}$ by
$\mathbb T^2\times D^2$, with $\partial D^2$ identified with the
$z$-circle, as in \cite[Section~5.1]{KRWY22}. The resulting torus manifold has a disk orbit space
and the prescribed two or three rods, so \cite{OR70} identifies
it with $\mathbb S^4$ or $\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^2$,
respectively. Removing the core torus gives the asserted
diffeomorphism types. The radial retraction $\rho\mapsto(1-s)\rho$,
$0\leqslant s\leqslant1$, retracts $X$ onto the cyclic union of
its fixed spheres, so $\pi_1(X)=\mathbb Z$.
In the hexagon case, by \cite{OR70}, the sphere $F$ over the middle rod has
\[
 [F]\cdot[F]
 =-\frac{\det(e_1,e_2)}{\det(e_1,e_1+e_2)\det(e_1+e_2,e_2)}=-1,
\]
as do the other fixed spheres, by the symmetry $\mathsf s$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:weyl}. In particular,
$X_{\mathrm{hex}}$ is not spin.

\emph{Curvature energy.} The removed torus has Euler characteristic zero, so the topology above gives $\chi(X)=\chi(\mathbb S^4)=2$ in the square case and $\chi(X)=\chi(\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^2)=3$ in the hexagon case, that is, $\chi(X)=\frac{m}{2}$.  By the differentiated Kasner asymptotics above, the hypersurfaces $\{\varsigma=S\}$ satisfy $\operatorname{Vol}\{\varsigma=S\}=O(S)$, $|\mathrm{II}|=O(S^{-1})$ and $|\operatorname{Rm}|=O(S^{-2})$, so the boundary term of the Chern-Gauss-Bonnet formula on $\{\varsigma\leqslant S\}$ is $O(S^{-2})$. Letting $S\to+\infty$ gives, in our normalization of $|\operatorname{Rm}|$,
\[
 \int_X|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\,dV=32\pi^2\chi(X)=16\pi^2m,
\]
which is the curvature energy of every $Z^{(k)}$, by Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-fundamental-groups}. So the blow-ups retain all the curvature energy.


\emph{Square identification.}
The equal-rod Euclidean Myers-Korotkin-Nicolai metric of \cite[Section~4.1]{KRWY22}, with  circle directions $e_1$ and $e_2$  of period $2\pi$  and quotiented by one period, has alternating rods with rod vectors $e_1$ and $e_2$, with endpoints equally spaced in $z$, angle $2\pi$ at the rods  and the untwisted angular identification. By \cite[Section~4.1, (4.5)]{KRWY22}, its diagonal shape tends to a constant as $\rho\to+\infty$. The symmetry exchanging the two circles  and shifting $z$  by one rod fixes this constant, so it equals $\Phi_o=I$. After a homothety, its Weyl period is $P_{\mathrm W}$, and the uniqueness argument above  identifies $g_{\mathrm{sq}}$ with the one-period quotient of  this metric.

\emph{Hexagonal geometry.}
If $g_{\mathrm{hex}}$ were static with respect to a torus generator $V$, then
$g_{\mathrm{hex}}(V,\cdot)/g_{\mathrm{hex}}(V,V)$ would be closed.
For any independent torus generator $W$, this makes
$g_{\mathrm{hex}}(V,W)/g_{\mathrm{hex}}(V,V)$ constant. Subtracting that multiple of $V$
from $W$ makes $G$ diagonal in a fixed real basis.
Its kernels along the rods could then have only two directions,
contradicting the three prescribed rod directions.

If $g_{\mathrm{hex}}$ were locally Hermitian in either orientation, $W^+$ would
have at most two eigenvalues. By \cite[Proposition~5(iv)]{Der83},
either $W^+\equiv0$ or $W^+$ is nowhere zero.
In the first case the universal cover is hyperk\"ahler and spin,
contradicting the lift of a fixed sphere of odd self-intersection.
In the second case, \cite[Proposition~2.1]{Li24} gives a Hermitian
non-K\"ahler structure on a cover of degree at most two, which is
still complete, Ricci-flat and of finite curvature energy.
Since its end has the Kasner asymptotics above, it contradicts
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{Li24}.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:covers}
The corner blow-ups $(M^{(k)},\Lambda_kg^{(k)},\widetilde c_k)$, with $\widetilde c_k$ over the corner $c_k$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:periodic-models},  converge to the infinite cyclic cover of $X$. Indeed,  the closed horizontal lift of one circuit of the orbit cylinder generates $\pi_1(X)=\mathbb Z$,  and the corresponding closed loop in $Z^{(k)}$ represents $\varpi_k$, which generates $\pi_1(Z^{(k)})=\mathbb Z_{k+1}$, by the generator calculation in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:weyl}, so its lift to $M^{(k)}$ closes only after $k+1$ circuits. Any fixed number of periods therefore lifts without identification for large $k$, and the limit has $z\in\mathbb R$. Its rods and corners repeat along $z$, so its curvature energy is infinite. The  estimates \eqref{eq:end-shape} and those following it still hold as $\rho\to+\infty$, while the Kasner end of Theorem~\ref{thm:periodic-models}  refers to the finite-period space $X$.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Since $\operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}\xi)=0$, we have $(S^{-1}\xi)^2=|\xi|_S^2I$ in 2D, and summing the exponential series gives the second equality in \eqref{eq:matrix-exp}. The first one is the exponential map of the Riemannian symmetric space of positive definite symmetric $2\times2$ matrices, with the metric $|\xi|_S^2$ above, \cite[Chapter~II.10]{BH99}, in which $\mathbb H^2=\{\det=1\}$ is totally geodesic; compare \cite[Appendix]{CS04}. (ii) If $W\in T_\Phi\mathbb H^2$ and $\Pi_SW=0$, then we have
\[
 W=cS,\qquad\text{and}\qquad 0=\operatorname{tr}(\Phi^{-1}W)=c\operatorname{tr}(\Phi^{-1}S)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=0,
\]
since $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi^{-1}S)>0$. If $\Phi=cS+U$ with $U\in T_S\mathbb H^2$, then $c=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}\Phi)>0$ and, since $S^{-1}U$ is trace-free, $1=\det\Phi=\det(cI+S^{-1}U)=c^2-|U|_S^2$. (iii) By the Koszul formula, the Levi-Civita connection of $g_{\mathbb H^2}$ is $\nabla_XY=dY(X)-\frac{1}{2}(X\Phi^{-1}Y+Y\Phi^{-1}X)$, and $(\Phi^{-1}\partial_j\Phi)^2=|\partial_j\Phi|_\Phi^2I$ as in (i). Hence, in an orthonormal frame, we compute
\[
 \tau_\gamma(\Phi)=\Delta_\gamma\Phi-\sum_j(\partial_j\Phi)\Phi^{-1}(\partial_j\Phi)
 =\Delta_\gamma\Phi-\tfrac12\sum_j\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\Phi^{-1}\partial_j\Phi)^2\bigr)\Phi,
\]
which is \eqref{eq:matrix-tension}. Equivalently, $\operatorname{div}_\gamma(\Phi^{-1}d\Phi)=\Phi^{-1}\tau_\gamma(\Phi)$, and $\rho^{-1}\operatorname{div}_\gamma(\rho\Phi^{-1}d\Phi)=\Phi^{-1}\bigl(\tau_\gamma(\Phi)+d\Phi(\nabla_\gamma\ell)\bigr)$ for $\ell=\log\rho$. Congruence covariance is immediate from the formulas.

title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Each division by $x$ is the formula $u/x=\int_0^1\partial_xu(tx,y)\,dt$, and $\|v(t\,\cdot,\cdot)\|_{C^{r,\alpha}}\leqslant\|v\|_{C^{r,\alpha}}$ for $0\leqslant t\leqslant1$ and similarly in $y$. For even $F$, apply it to the odd function $\partial_xF$. For the last identity of \eqref{eq:divided-odd}, $f(t):=tx\,\partial_xu(tx,y)-u(tx,y)$ satisfies $f(0)=0$ and $f'(t)=tx^2\,\partial_x^2u(tx,y)$.

(b) Consider first one radial variable $x=|Z|$, with $z$ denoting the remaining coordinates, and put $n:=Z/|Z|$ for $Z\neq0$. A bounded extension from a fixed signed coordinate rectangle, followed by averaging with the prescribed parity and an even cutoff, reduces the estimates to compactly supported profiles, which we first assume smooth. Their lifts are then smooth by \cite{Whi43} and part~(a).

Scalar lifting preserves $C^{0,\alpha}$, since $\bigl||Z|-|\widetilde Z|\bigr|\leqslant|Z-\widetilde Z|$. If moreover $v(0,z)=0$ and $H$ is smooth on the unit sphere, then, extending the product by $0$ at $Z=0$, we have
\[
 \|H(n)\,v(|Z|,z)\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\leqslant C\|H\|_{C^1}\|v\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}:
\]
for two points off the axis, at distance $d$ and with smaller radius $\varsigma$, the change of the angular factor contributes at most $C[v]_\alpha\varsigma^\alpha\min\{1,d/\varsigma\}\leqslant C[v]_\alpha d^\alpha$. This proves the estimates of order $0$. For order $1$, use
\[
 \partial_{Z_i}\varphi(|Z|,z)=n_i\,\varphi_x(|Z|,z),\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \partial_{Z_i}\bigl(n_a\,u(|Z|,z)\bigr)=\delta_{ia}v(|Z|,z)+n_in_a\,w(|Z|,z),
\]
where $v:=u/x=\int_0^1u_x(tx,\cdot)\,dt$ and $w:=u_x-v$. Here $\varphi_x$ and $w$ vanish at $x=0$, and $\|v\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|w\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\leqslant C\|u\|_{C^{1,\alpha}}$. Tangential derivatives commute with the lifts and preserve parity, so the estimates of order $0$ apply to them.

Write $\mathcal L$ for either lift and $D$ for its one-block operator, $\partial_x^2+jx^{-1}\partial_x+\Delta_z$, respectively $\partial_x^2+x^{-1}\partial_x-x^{-2}+\Delta_z$. The polar formula for the Laplacian and $\Delta_{\mathbb S^1}n_a=-n_a$ give $\Delta\mathcal Lf=\mathcal L(Df)$. Part~(a) shows that $D$ preserves parity and $\|Df\|_{C^{r-2,\alpha}}\leqslant C\|f\|_{C^{r,\alpha}}$. For $r\geqslant2$, induction on $r$ and the interior Schauder estimate \cite[Theorem~6.2]{GT01} on unit balls give
\[
 \|\mathcal Lf\|_{C^{r,\alpha}}\leqslant C\bigl(\|\mathcal L(Df)\|_{C^{r-2,\alpha}}+\|\mathcal Lf\|_{C^0}\bigr)\leqslant C\|f\|_{C^{r,\alpha}}.
\]
A parity-preserving mollification removes the smoothness assumption, by compactness in $C^{r,\alpha'}$, $\alpha'<\alpha$, and lower semicontinuity of the H\"older seminorm. The corner case follows by applying the one-block result in each variable, and restriction to the signed coordinate planes gives the reverse bounds. The Laplacian identities pass to the limit for $r\geqslant2$.

(c) The identities \eqref{eq:lift-energy} follow from $dZ\,d{Z'}=x^jy^j\,dx\,dy\,d\sigma_{{\mathbb S^j}}\,d\sigma_{{\mathbb S^j}}$ and $|\nabla\mathcal L_\perp u|^2=|du|_0^2+(x^{-2}+y^{-2})u^2$. Let $P$ be the average over $O(j+1)\times O(j+1)$ for the scalar lift, and over the action of $O(2)\times O(2)$ for the tensor lift. A smooth averaged test function is the lift of an even, respectively odd, profile. For the tensor lift, it has the form $Z_aZ'_b\varphi_0(|Z|,|Z'|)$ with $\varphi_0$ smooth and even. By \eqref{eq:lift-energy}, the weak pairing with such a lift is the weighted pairing on the quadrant. Since the lifted operator $\widetilde L$ and forcing $\widetilde F$ are equivariant, for the lift $\Xi$ of a weak solution and every compactly supported smooth test function $\vartheta$, we have
\[
 \langle\widetilde L\Xi-\widetilde F,\vartheta\rangle=\langle\widetilde L\Xi-\widetilde F,P\vartheta\rangle=0,
\]
and \eqref{eq:lift-energy} extends this to the energy completions.

For the third line, the singular part of $d\ell-2ds$ is $3\,dx/x-dy/y$, and
\[
 \frac{x}y\Bigl(\Delta_0+\frac{3}x\partial_x-\frac{1}y\partial_y\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{y}x\widehat\omega\Bigr)=D_\perp\widehat\omega,\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_\Phi=e^{-\widehat s}\bigl[d\widehat\omega+\widehat\omega(-dx/x+dy/y)\bigr].
\]

In \eqref{eq:connection-form-local}, the coefficients of $A_\Phi$ have parities (even, odd) and (odd, even), so $|A_\Phi|^2$ is even. label: lem:lifted-target
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lifted-target}
Let $U$ be a rod (resp. corner) chart for the fixed smooth background of Lemma~\ref{lem:shifted-regularity}, and $U'\subset U$ a chart whose closure in the closed half-plane (resp. quadrant) is a compact subset of $U$. Let $\xi$, with $\mathfrak a_2(\xi;U)<+\infty$ in \eqref{cmp:positive-forms}, be a weak solution of $A_2\xi=F_2$ on $U$ in this local energy class, with $F_s\in C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}(U)$ and $F_\perp\in C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}(U)$. Then we have
\[
 \|\xi_s\|_{C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}(U')}+\|\xi_\perp\|_{C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}(U')}
 \leqslant C\bigl(\|F_s\|_{C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm{ev}}(U)}+\|F_\perp\|_{C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm{odd}}(U)}+\|\xi\|_{L^2(U,\rho\,dA_\gamma)}\bigr),
\]
where $C$ depends only on $U$, $U'$ and the background.

label: cmp:frame-jacobi
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\xi=\xi_se_s+\xi_\perp e_\perp$ in the frame \eqref{eq:target-rod-frame}, whose connection form $A_\Phi:=e^{-s}d\omega$ has the regularized expression \eqref{eq:connection-form-local}. Then we have
\[
 \nabla\xi=(d\xi_s+\xi_\perp A_\Phi)\,e_s+(d\xi_\perp-\xi_sA_\Phi)\,e_\perp,\qquad\text{and}\qquad d\Phi=ds\,e_s+A_\Phi\,e_\perp.
\]
The background map equation gives $\operatorname{div}_{\rho\,dA_\gamma}A_\Phi^\sharp=\langle A_\Phi,ds\rangle_\gamma$. With it, \eqref{eq:weighted-Jacobi} takes the symmetric form
\begin{equation}\label{cmp:frame-jacobi}
 A_2=\begin{pmatrix}L_0-2|A_\Phi|_\gamma^2-1&T_0^*\\ T_0&L_0-|ds|_\gamma^2-|A_\Phi|_\gamma^2-1\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
in the basis $(\xi_s,\xi_\perp)$, with $L_0:=\Delta_\gamma+\langle d\ell,d\,\cdot\,\rangle_\gamma$ and $T_0:=-2\langle A_\Phi,d\,\cdot\,\rangle_\gamma$, where $T_0^*$ is the formal adjoint of $T_0$ for $\rho\,dA_\gamma$. The zeroth-order coefficients are those of $\mathfrak a_2$ in \eqref{cmp:positive-forms}.

Write $x=|Z|$, $y=|{Z'}|$ for $Z,{Z'}\in\mathbb R^2$, and lift the two components of $\xi$ from the quadrant to a scalar and a tensor field on $\widetilde U:=\{(Z,Z')\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2:(|Z|,|Z'|)\in U\}$ by
\[
 \Xi_s:=\mathcal L_1\xi_s,\qquad \Xi_\perp:=\mathcal L_\perp\xi_\perp,\qquad\text{that is}\quad
 (\Xi_\perp)_{ab}(Z,{Z'})=\frac{Z_a}x\frac{{Z'}_b}y\,\xi_\perp(x,y).
\]
For the fixed smooth background, $\mathfrak t:=\widehat\omega/(xy)$ is smooth and even, by Corollary~\ref{cor:fixed-set-regularity} and Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(a) with $k=l=1$, and we write
\[
 s=\log(y/x)+\widehat s,\qquad P:=e^{-\widehat s}\frac{\partial_x\mathfrak t}x,\qquad Q:=e^{-\widehat s}(2\mathfrak t+y\partial_y\mathfrak t),\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_\Phi=x^2yP\,dx+xQ\,dy,
\]
with $P$ and $Q$ smooth and even.
Direct computations in the variables $(Z,{Z'})$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:angular-energy}
\begin{aligned}
 |\nabla\Xi_\perp|^2&=|d\xi_\perp|_0^2+(x^{-2}+y^{-2})\xi_\perp^2,\\
 |ds|_0^2-x^{-2}-y^{-2}&=|d\widehat s|_0^2-2\frac{\partial_x\widehat s}x+2\frac{\partial_y\widehat s}y.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The formula for $\nabla\xi$ above, the identity $|\xi\wedge d\Phi|=|\xi_sA_\Phi-\xi_\perp ds|$, the boundedness of $A_\Phi$ and \eqref{eq:angular-energy} give $\|\Xi\|_{H^1(\widetilde U)}^2\leqslant C\,\mathfrak a_2(\xi;U)$. The right-hand side of the second identity of \eqref{eq:angular-energy} is smooth by evenness and \eqref{eq:divided-even}. In the transverse component of $A_2\xi=F_2$, the operator $D_1-|ds|_0^2$ therefore lifts to the Euclidean Laplacian on $\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2$ plus a smooth potential.

By \eqref{cmp:frame-jacobi}, the off-diagonal entries of $A_2$ are $T_0=-2\langle A_\Phi,d\,\cdot\,\rangle_\gamma$, from $\xi_s$ to $\xi_\perp$, and its formal adjoint $T_0^*$ for $\rho\,dA_\gamma$. After lifting, $e^{2c_\gamma}T_0=-2\langle A_\Phi,d\,\cdot\,\rangle_0$ becomes
\begin{equation}\label{app:lifted-coupling}
\begin{aligned}
 &\bigl[\mathcal L_\perp\bigl(-2\langle A_\Phi,d\xi_s\rangle_0\bigr)\bigr]_{ab}=-2Z_a\bigl[P\,Z'_b\,(Z\cdot\nabla_Z\Xi_s)+Q\,\partial_{Z'_b}\Xi_s\bigr],
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
whose coefficients are smooth. The measure $\rho\,dA_\gamma$ lifts to a constant multiple of the smooth positive density $e^{\widehat\ell+2c_\gamma}dZ\,dZ'$, so the formal adjoint $T_0^*$ for this measure also has smooth coefficients. The remaining diagonal terms are smooth.
Thus the lifted equation has the form
\[
 \Delta\Xi+B^a\partial_a\Xi+C\Xi=\bigl(\mathcal L_1(e^{2c_\gamma}F_s),\mathcal L_\perp(e^{2c_\gamma}F_\perp)\bigr),\qquad\text{with }B^a,C\ \text{smooth}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(c), the lifted system holds weakly across the axes.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:division-lifts}(b), its right-hand side is $C^{0,\alpha}$, and interior elliptic regularity for this system with scalar Laplacian principal part, followed by the Schauder estimate \cite[Chapters~6 and~9]{GT01}, gives the asserted bound.
Restriction to $Z=(x,0)$, ${Z'}=(y,0)$, with signed $x,y$, gives the even extension of $\xi_s$ and the odd extension of $\xi_\perp$.

label: lem:B-cutoffs
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{lem:B-cutoffs}Let $p_0$ be a point of a two-dimensional chart with the metric $\gamma_\beta$, for $\beta$ in a compact subset of $(0,+\infty)$. Let $A$ be bounded and uniformly elliptic, $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $\operatorname{div}(A\,du)=f$ holds weakly off $p_0$, then it holds weakly across $p_0$. The same conclusion holds if the measure is multiplied by a density bounded above and below by positive constants.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varrho$ be the radial coordinate of a cone chart centered at $p_0$, which is $R$ for the central chart. The logarithmic cutoffs $\chi_\varepsilon:=\min\bigl\{1,\max\bigl\{0,\lambda_\varepsilon\bigr\}\bigr\}$, with $\lambda_\varepsilon:=\log(\varrho/\varepsilon^2)/\log(1/\varepsilon)$, vanish near $p_0$, converge to $1$ off $p_0$, and satisfy, by polar integration, for every compactly supported smooth $\varphi$,
\[
 \int\varphi^2|d\chi_\varepsilon|^2\leqslant\frac{C_\varphi}{\log(1/\varepsilon)},\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \Bigl|\int\varphi\langle A\,du,d\chi_\varepsilon\rangle\Bigr|\leqslant C\|du\|_{L^2(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)}\|\varphi\,d\chi_\varepsilon\|_{L^2}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Testing the equation with $\chi_\varepsilon\varphi$ and dominated convergence give the weak equation across $p_0$. The cutoff estimate persists for such a density, and radial cutoffs preserve the finite symmetries.
